articles.title: Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi bring progress on prisoners but not on peace
articles.summary:
US envoys to visit Moscow and Dublin on Thursday for talks with Vladimir Putin and Volodymyr Zelenskyy respectively

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to the “largest prisoner exchange” of the…

blocks.text: Russia and Ukraine have agreed to the “largest prisoner exchange” of the war at their first US-brokered talks since February but made little progress towards a broader peace agreement.
Both sides sent senior delegations to the two-day talks, led by Donald Trump’s envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, in an effort to find a solution to end the nearly-five-year war.

David Arakhamia, a senior member of Ukraine’s delegation, said the Russian team had arrived with “very, very strict directives”, making it difficult to narrow differences. But he said there had been “really big progress” on security guarantees for Ukraine after the war. “I think we have good momentum to bring about a solution before the new year,” Arakhamia said.

blocks.caption: Kushner, left, and Witkoff confer during a briefing after the talks. Photograph: Altaf Qadri/AP

blocks.text: Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, also struck an upbeat tone, saying he could see a path to an agreement. “These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex. It’s a very hot war,” he said. “But we see all the different ingredients to make a deal. We just have to figure out how to refine those ingredients, organise them and create the right structure and pathway.”
Kushner said the planned exchange, expected to involve more than 1,000 prisoners from each side, would “reunite families, build trust and create momentum towards peace”.

The US envoys are due to travel to Moscow on Thursday to discuss the Abu Dhabi talks with Vladimir Putin, before heading to Dublin, where they are expected to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy and a group of European partners.

“In close coordination with Ukraine and our European partners, we have aligned on proposals we will discuss with President Putin in Moscow tomorrow, followed by consultations with President Zelenskyy,” Kushner said.
But despite the optimism, Kushner also said the two sides had yet to resolve their territorial dispute.

Russia’s territorial demands have shifted over time, but Moscow has made clear it wants control of all the Donbas, including areas still held by Kyiv, as well as the parts of two southern regions it does not yet occupy.

blocks.caption: Vladimir Medinsky addresses a press conference in Abu Dhabi. Photograph: Oleg Kozyritskiy/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Vladimir Medinsky, the hardline Russian official who led Moscow’s delegation, said that “every inch of our land will be returned to Russia, one way or another,” in a sign that Moscow was unwilling to soften its territorial demands. Russia would be satisfied with the negotiations only “when there is peace on its terms”, he added.
He also said the main task was to create a new security system in Europe that would become “a new Yalta and Potsdam”.

Medinsky said Europe’s post-second world war security system was failing, with Ukraine merely the place where its wider problems had erupted. “Essentially, the whole body is sick, and Ukraine was just a cyst that burst. The whole body must be cured. A Band-Aid won’t be enough,” Medinsky said.

His focus on Europe’s wider security order is likely to heighten concern among European leaders that Washington and Moscow could reach a broader agreement on the continent’s security, potentially limiting Nato’s military presence in eastern Europe.

Russia appears to be seeking to revive demands it presented to Nato in 2021, including a halt to further enlargement that would rule out Ukraine’s membership, restrictions on Nato forces and weapons in European countries that joined after 1997, and limits on missile deployments.
That ultimatum was dismissed as a non-starter by the west and, weeks later, Russia invaded Ukraine.

Concerned that Europe’s security future could be discussed over their heads, European governments sent envoys to Abu Dhabi to try to influence the talks, although they are not believed to have taken part directly.

Medinsky dismissed their presence, saying that if they had come “as tourists”, they could talk in the hotel lobby, and that Russia would consider proposals only if they had “something specific” to offer.

European leaders have increasingly discussed the need for a direct channel to Putin, but no clear candidate has emerged. The leaders of Norway and Finland have recently spoken to the Russian president, while Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said on Wednesday that he was open to doing so.

Kushner, meanwhile, said Europe should choose a single representative to speak on its behalf. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said.

blocks.caption: Smoke billows after a drone attack near Ust-Luga in Russia’s Leningrad region. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters

blocks.text: He stressed that one of the aims of his trip to Moscow was to “see if we can get Europeans added” to future talks. “The issues that were covered in these discussions were really postwar security,” he said. “How do we make sure that once this war ends, it doesn’t start again?”

Russian officials have long opposed European participation, arguing that countries supplying weapons to Kyiv cannot act as impartial mediators. Medinsky said Russia would speak to European countries only “when their conscience awakens” and they stop supplying Ukraine with weapons.

As diplomatic efforts continued, both sides kept up their attacks. Russia launched drones at Kyiv and other regions during the day, while Ukraine struck the Ust-Luga port on Russia’s Baltic coast overnight. The port, in the Leningrad region, is a major route for Russian energy exports and was still burning on Wednesday.

articles.title: Jim Jordan, once called a 'legislative terrorist' by a top Republican, will now lead the party in U.S. House
articles.summary: The Republicans may have just lost control of the House of Representatives in resounding fashion, but they signalled Tuesday they may not be in a conciliatory mood with Democrats, picking combative…

image.caption: Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan addresses reporters Tuesday on Capitol Hill in Washington after his election as House Republican leader. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: The Republicans may have just lost control of the House of Representatives in resounding fashion, but they signalled Tuesday they may not be in a conciliatory mood with Democrats, picking combative Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan as their leader in the chamber.

Jordan, a longtime ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, emerged from a closed-door session with party colleagues Tuesday as the winner over Rep. Steve Scalise of Louisiana to become House minority leader.
Jordan, 62, said Republicans would focus on fighting for American families over the next two years.
“When Democrats offer more government, we’ll offer more freedom,” he said. “We will bring that fight in committee, on the floor and on the stump every single day.”
'A pitbull who will fight it out'

Jordan, once described as the "walking embodiment of conflict-mindedness" by a member of the conservative Federalist Society, was first elected to Congress in 2006. He was seen as one of the prime Republicans legislators responsible for a 16-day shutdown in late 2013 over a government funding bill, in opposition to plans from Barack Obama's administration to push ahead with landmark health-care legislation.

Not seeing his party's leadership as sufficiently to the right, Jordan soon founded the House Freedom Caucus with Ron DeSantis, Mark Meadows (North Carolina) and Mick Mulvaney (South Carolina). DeSantis would eventually leave Congress for two terms as Florida governor, while Meadows and Mulvaney served in the first Trump administration.
Trump loyalists gear up for a fight after Democratic ‘blue-nami’
John Boehner, the former Republican House Speaker from Ohio who often bore the brunt of appeals from that caucus, once described Jordan as a "legislative terrorist."
"I just never saw a guy who spent more time tearing things apart — never building anything, never putting anything together," Boehner told CBS News in a 2021 interview.
Boehner's comments may not have been just a matter of a retired politician settling scores.

Two years ago, the Center for Effective Lawmaking rated Jordan 202nd out of 205 House Republicans in terms of legislative effectiveness. The ongoing joint project between the University of Virginia and Vanderbilt University examines a number of criteria, including number of bills sponsored, whether the bills made it into or out of committees, and whether they were subsequently passed by the House.

items: Republicans took big hits in the U.S. midterms. Does that mean Trump's political era is over?
JD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?

blocks.text: Passing legislation is never the prime responsibility of a minority leader however, as Alyssa Farah Griffin hinted at in a post on Tuesday. Griffin, who served in the first Trump administration and is now a panelist on The View, praised Jordan's elevation.

"In the new Congress, House Republicans will have very little actual power," she said. "They need a pitbull who will fight it out with Democrats, and on TV and who has the ear of the [White House]. That’s Jim Jordan."
LISTEN | Our CBC Washington correspondents map out post-midterm possibilities:
Two Blocks from the White House31:02The U.S. midterms are over. Now what?
Defied subpoena from Democrats
Democratic legislators and pundits argued Jordan’s selection suggested that Republicans aren't receiving the message sent to them last week in the midterms.
Democrats so far have gained a new total of 42 seats in the 435-member House — they have flipped 44 Republican seats, while Republicans flipped 2 Democrat seats — with 13 races yet to be called.

“I would think that they would want somebody that was going to moderate towards what the voters want. They lost so many Republican voters,” said Rep. Pramila Jayapal, a Democrat from Washington. “Obviously that’s not the case.”
How did things go so wrong for Jim Jordan? | About That

Former U.S. senator and Saturday Night Live cast member Al Franken quipped on social media: "Picking Jim Jordan to be Minority Leader is surviving Republican House members saying, 'We heard you, America!'"

Jordan has been a vigorous defender of the current president, excoriating special counsel investigations into Trump's 2016 campaign contacts with Russia and his handling of classified documents as a private citizen. Leading up to Trump's 2019 impeachment related to foreign policy with Ukraine, Jordan encouraged a group of Republicans who stormed a closed-door deposition, a move Lindsey Graham, the late Republican senator from South Carolina, called "nuts."

Jordan ran for House Speaker in 2023, but couldn't get the necessary votes. Some lawmakers reported they had received threats of violence in emails and phone calls from citizens supporting Jordan's effort.

In a social media post Tuesday, Ayanna Pressley, Democratic representative from Massachusetts, highlighted what she saw as a number of Jordan's failings, leading with his activities supporting Trump's election denialism after his 2020 loss to Joe Biden.

House Republicans just made Jim Jordan their Minority Leader. The same guy who: —Helped plan & execute Jan 6 —Has covered up the Epstein files —Wants to ban abortion nationwide —Voted to gut Social Security & Medicare —Is a Trump loyalist Republicans are doubling down on far-right, MAGA extremism.—RepPressley

The committee with seven Democrats and two Republicans that examined the 2020 election and the lead-up to the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the Capitol said in its final report that Jordan led a conference call four days earlier "in which he, President Trump, and other members of Congress discussed strategies for delaying the Jan. 6 joint session" to certify Biden's win.

The panel wanted to hear more from Jordan about his communications with the White House during those feverish days, but he defied a subpoena. Despite that fact, in his time as a leading Republican member of the House's judiciary and oversight committees, Jordan has frequently been in favour of issuing subpoenas to elicit testimony in Congress.
Trump honoured Jordan five days after the Capitol riot with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, praising him as "an inspiration to freedom-loving Americans everywhere."
Denied knowledge of abuse allegations

Jordan might also be considered an interesting choice in terms of optics, given how prominently Jeffrey Epstein figured in hundreds of midterm campaign ads before the convicted sex offender died in 2019. On the same day Jordan was named minority leader, a Republican-led committee issued a report finding fault with the Trump administration's handling of the Epstein files, with the release leading to some female victims and accusers having their identities revealed when their names should have been redacted.

Jordan, a two-time NCAA wrestling champion at Ohio State, later served as an assistant coach for the university from 1986 to 1994. That period of time encompassed a small portion of a two-decade period in which a physician who worked for the school's athletic department was alleged to have sexually abused athletes.
Watch: Miller move shows White House not looking to moderate:
Some former wrestlers say Jordan was among those who knew of the allegations and failed to intervene in a meaningful way, though Jordan has denied any such knowledge of any abuse taking place.

In 2022, when reports emerged that a 10-year-old Ohio girl had to travel across state lines to get an abortion after being raped, Jordan suggested in a social media post that it was "another lie" from Democratic and progressive factions. He deleted the tweet after the allegations were confirmed.

items: Republicans block impeachment push against Pete Hegseth

blocks.text: As the Republicans settled on Jordan in the House on Tuesday, their Senate colleagues voted to keep John Thune as their leader in that chamber.

The Democrats have yet to formally deliberate on who will lead them as House Speaker and Senate majority leader in the next Congress. The House leadership decision is expected next week, with the Democratic senators to vote for their leaders in early December.

articles.title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
articles.summary: Bessent is now one of several Trump administration officials to live on military bases due to safety concerns.

blocks.text: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports.
CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal.
Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade.
While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials.

"After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.
Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents.
Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area.
In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.
The BBC has contacted the White House for comment.
In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans.
The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".

Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year.

Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard.

The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.

In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after the Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade.

articles.title: Democracy study: One-quarter of Germans want a right-wing authoritarian dictatorship
articles.summary: The far-right AfD's electoral successes point to a new trend in Germany: Prejudice, resentment, and extremism are on the rise. A new study suggests satisfaction with democracy is at a low ebb.

image.caption: Germany's Constitution, the Basic Law, is the foundation of its free democratic orderImage: Joko/Bildagentur-online/picture alliance

blocks.text: Satisfaction with democracy in Germany has hit a new low, while the past is being idealized, and people are expressing a longing for a radical break. The longing for an authoritarian leader and antisemitic sentiments are also on the rise. These are key findings of the authoritarianism study presented Wednesday in Berlin, which has been conducted every two years since 2002.

The study, led by the Else Frenkel-Brunswik Institute for Democracy Research at the University of Leipzig, is based on the answers to a questionnaire sent in by over 900 respondents, who the researchers say are a representative cross-section of the German population.

For the first time since the study series began, approval of democracy as an idea fell just below the 90% mark, which, the study said, is primarily attributable to a loss of trust among respondents in the former East Germany (85.7%). The decline in approval of democracy as experienced in everyday life is even more severe: Nationwide, only one-third are satisfied with democracy, with figures having fallen sharply in both the East (22.8%) and the West (36%).
Does Germany's Gen Z still feel the East-West divide?
'Our democracy is under great pressure'

The growing rejection of democracy is also reflected in the desire for some kind of authoritarian nationalist government: Just under a quarter of respondents explicitly supported the idea of a "single strong party that embodies the national community as a whole." In the east, the figure stands at 30.9%, above the Germany-wide average of 22.3%.

"Our democracy is under great pressure. It has lost acceptance among the general population. It is alarming how much an authoritarian yearning is taking its place," concluded social psychologist and study author Oliver Decker.
Nationalism reaches record high

Far-right attitudes have risen for the second consecutive year. Of particular note in the study was what the researchers called a chauvinistic national pride, which, with 19.9% approval, has reached its highest level since the study series began. The proportion of people with a consistently far-right worldview has reached 6.9%, the highest level since 2014, the study found.

Just under 15% of respondents said they explicitly believe that "everything has to fall apart so that something new can emerge," while nearly one in three respondents believes that "something radical is needed for the current state of affairs to change." Another 29.1% agree with this to some extent.
Amid far right's rise, is Germany at a breaking point?
Connection between far right and AfD

According to the study, those who share this yearning for catastrophe exhibit significantly more antisemitic sentiments, both things linked to a preference for certain political parties. The study found that a large proportion of eligible voters with this orientation favor the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD).

"Through its violent rhetoric, the AfD promises to realize the political goals of far-right ideology," the study said. The party's form and content, in other words, correspond exactly to the message that a significant portion of the population wants to hear. "It offers a political home to those who adhere to far-right thinking, while at the same time presenting itself as capable of connecting with a broad segment of society."
Antisemitic attitudes doubled

Study co-author Johannes Kiess calls on political leaders at all levels to find countermeasures. "The rejection of the present state of the world must be countered with compelling democratic alternatives and the ability to take political action today," he said. This also applies to the significant rise in antisemitism, which has more than doubled since 2022.

When asked about the motives behind antisemitic attitudes, the results show that for 16 percent of respondents, the policies of the Israeli government are the decisive factor. This, too, is a record high in the context of the long-term study. While the figure in 2020 was significantly higher in the east (12%) than in the west (8.4%), the figures have since converged. Antisemitism related to Israel is actually slightly stronger in the West than in the East.
Elif Eralp: From daughter of refugees to Berlin mayor?
Hostility toward Muslims is also on the rise

Hostility toward Muslims is also on the rise. It peaked at over 40% in 2018, before dropping to well below 30%, and currently stands at 34.1%. These figures are based on two statements respondents were asked to agree with in each survey: "Muslims should be prohibited from immigrating to Germany" and "because of the many Muslims here, I sometimes feel like a stranger in my own country."

Misogyny is another issue regularly surveyed in the study. In the current survey, 18.3% agreed with anti-feminist statements. Notably, until now, a higher proportion of East Germans had been opposed to feminist causes. As recently as 2024, the difference between the East (34.6%) and the West (19.6%) was enormous. Two years later, the figure in the East has halved to 17.8%, while in western Germany it has fallen only slightly to 18.4%.
A glimmer of hope

Despite the negative trend, there is a glimmer of hope at the end of the Leipzig Authoritarianism Study: While the results are "alarming," long-term trends show that a reversal of this trend is possible: "In earlier surveys, far-right statements already achieved high approval ratings, which then declined again in subsequent years. In addition to the influence of societal crises, political action and its societal perception are of central importance."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
articles.summary: The news comes at a turbulent time for Prabowo, who faces a growing rift with his predecessor Joko Widodo.

blocks.text: Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.

Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.

Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.

Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.

Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.

All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

articles.title: Kenya's last Ebola patient leaves hospital
articles.summary: Kenya had nine confirmed cases, while DR Congo continues to battle its deadliest outbreak of the disease.

image.caption: Nairobi Hospital opened an Ebola isolation unit in response to the outbreak [File: October 2026]Image: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Kenyan Health Minister Aden Duale said on Wednesday that the east African country had discharged its last remaining Ebola patient from a Nairobi hospital.
The final person to undergo treatment for the disease in Kenya had 11 contact cases, Duale said, who will also undergo 21 days of quarantine.
Kenya will be declared Ebola-free on December 23 if no one else exhibits symptoms until then.
"Through strengthened surveillance and contact tracing, all 135 contacts linked to the index case were successfully traced and monitored," the health ministry said.
"All nine confirmed cases remained within a single transmission cluster, with no community transmission recorded," it added.
Did Ebola start spreading before officials even knew?
The first of its nine cases, reported on October 6, came from a Kenyan man who had recently travelled back from the Demoratic Republic of Congo.
Seven patients recovered, and two passed away.
What is the state of the Ebola outbreak?
DR Congo on Wednesday reported 11,000 cases of the virulent, often fatal disease.
This current outbreak, which began in May, has become Congo's deadliest, claiming 5,387 lives so far.
There has also been one case reported in Nigeria, from a patient who had recently travelled from Uganda, which saw a small cluster of the disease.

articles.title: SWS: Awareness of ASEAN high among Filipino adults; net trust rating 'moderate'
articles.summary: At least 91% of Filipino adults are aware of the regional organization of countries, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but the net trust is classified as moderate at +25, according…

blocks.text: At least 91% of Filipino adults are aware of the regional organization of countries, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), but the net trust is classified as moderate at +25, according to the Third Quarter 2026 Social Weather Survey released on Wednesday.

The Survey, conducted on September 21-27, 2026, found that among those aware of ASEAN, 46% (correctly rounded) had much trust in it, while 21% (correctly rounded) had little trust, for a net trust rating (% much trust minus % little trust) of +25, classified by SWS as moderate..

At least 13% had very much trust, and 32% had somewhat much trust. Another 16% had somewhat little trust, and 4% had very little trust. Another 31% were undecided, and 3% did not know or refused to answer.
The Third Quarter 2026 Social Weather Survey was conducted from September 21 to 27, 2026, and the First Quarter 2026 Social Weather Survey from March 24 to 31, 2026.

Each used face-to-face interviews of 1,500 adults (18 years old and above) nationwide: 600 in Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila) and 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. The sampling error margins are ±3% for national percentages, ±4% for Balance Luzon, and ±6% each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao.
Higher net trust in ASEAN in 2013 and 2017
The net trust in ASEAN was a good +30 (50% much, 20% little) in September 2013 and a good +41 (56% much, 14% little, correctly rounded) in June 2017, higher than the moderate +25 in September 2026.
Meanwhile, the awareness of ASEAN was 94% in September 2013 and 98% in June 2017, compared with 91% in September 2026.
The net trust in ASEAN was a moderate +29 in Metro Manila, a moderate +28 in Balance Luzon, a moderate +24 (correctly rounded) in the Visayas, and a moderate +18 (correctly rounded) in Mindanao.

Net trust in ASEAN rose with education: it was a neutral +8 among non-elementary graduates, a moderate +12 among elementary graduates, a moderate +26 among junior high school graduates, a good +35 among those with some senior high school up to some college, and a good +45 among college graduates.
For the question on prior awareness of the hosting, the highest percentage was in Metro Manila at 42%, followed by 28% in the Visayas, 27% in Balance Luzon, and 20% in Mindanao.

Prior awareness rose with education, with 12% among non-elementary graduates, 21% among elementary graduates, 29% among junior high school graduates, 32% among those with some senior high school up to some college, and 55% among college graduates.
Awareness of the Philippines’ hosting of the 2026 ASEAN

The First Quarter 2026 Social Weather Survey, conducted on March 24-31, 2026, found 28% of adult Filipinos previously aware that the Philippines was hosting the 2026 ASEAN leaders’ meetings. The remaining 72% heard about it only during the interview.
Most adult Filipinos, at 91% are expecting that the Philippines will benefit from hosting the regional meetings.
At least 21% expected the country will benefit very much, 52% who expected it to benefit much, and 17% who expected it to benefit a little. The remaining 9% did not expect the Philippines to benefit.
In contrast, when the Philippines last hosted the ASEAN leaders’ meetings in 2017, 95% in September 2016 and 94% in June 2017 expected the country to benefit.
Those who did not expect the Philippines to benefit were 5% in September 2016 and 5% in June 2017, compared with 9% in March 2026.
Meanwhile, those who expected the Philippines to benefit from hosting were 92% in Metro Manila, 91% in Balance Luzon, 90% in Mindanao, and 89% in the Visayas.
The highest was in Metro Manila at 28%, followed by the Visayas at 26%, Balance Luzon at 20%, and Mindanao at 18%.

By education, those who expected the Philippines to benefit ranged from 87% among non-elementary graduates to 93% each among those with some senior high school up to some college and among college graduates.
Among those previously aware of the hosting, 94% expected the Philippines to benefit, compared with 89% of those who heard about it only during the interview.
The share who expected it to benefit very much was significantly higher among those previously aware (34%) than among those who heard about it only during the interview (17%).
Issues to prioritize in ASEAN meetings
The First Quarter 2026 survey also asked adult Filipinos, in an open-ended question allowing up to three responses, what issues the Philippines should prioritize as the ASEAN host this year.
The most mentioned were the following:

items: rising prices of goods and inflation at 19%
the West Philippine Sea at 16%
oil prices and supply at 12%
poverty at 9%
economic and financial crisis at 6%

blocks.text: They were followed by jobs and livelihood at 5%, war and conflict at 4%, crime and illegal drugs and food supply and hunger at 3% each, and security and safety at 2%. Another 19% mentioned other issues, each cited by 2% or less.
However, 12% said there was no issue to prioritize, and 13% did not know or refused to answer.
Top issue was rising prices in Balance Luzon and Mindanao, and the West Philippine Sea in Metro Manila and the Visayas

Rising prices of goods and inflation was the most mentioned issue in Mindanao at 23% and in Balance Luzon at 20%. The West Philippine Sea was the most mentioned in Metro Manila at 22% and in the Visayas at 16%.
Oil prices and supply were mentioned by 15% each in Metro Manila and Balance Luzon, 10% in Mindanao, and 4% in the Visayas.
Those who said there was no issue to prioritize, or who did not know or refused to answer, were highest in the Visayas, at 17% and 19%, respectively.

Rising prices of goods and inflation was the most mentioned issue among non-elementary graduates at 22%, elementary graduates at 20%, and junior high school graduates at 21%. The West Philippine Sea was the most mentioned among those with some senior high school up to some college at 24% and among college graduates at 21%.
Mentions of the West Philippine Sea were 3% among non-elementary graduates, 11% among elementary graduates, and 18% among junior high school graduates.

Those who said there was no issue to prioritize were 19% among non-elementary graduates and 7% among college graduates. Those who did not know or refused to answer were 16% among non-elementary graduates and 7% among college graduates. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Argentine lawyer mocks UK’s sovereignty claim in Falklands oil case
articles.summary:
Lawyer says Britain wrong to believe in historic doctrine that Crown has sovereignty over parts of oceans

Britain should not be permitted to act as a 17th century colonial power treating the…

blocks.text: Britain should not be permitted to act as a 17th-century colonial power treating the waters around the Falkland Islands as a Dominium maris Britannici, Argentina has told an international tribunal.

Marcelo Kohen, representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked Britain for apparently believing in the historic doctrine that the British crown has sovereignty over expansive parts of the oceans.

Argentina has applied to the international tribunal for the law of the sea (Itlos) for a ruling that would force Britain to suspend the drilling for oil in the North Basin of the Falkland Islands ahead of further arbitration.
The Sea Lion oilfield is about 130 miles north of the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory over which Argentina has a longstanding sovereignty claim.

Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, reportedly shared among his cabinet a photograph of the Argentinian legal team in Hamburg, describing it as “tremendous”, adding that “we are working on the Falklands issue like no one else in history”.

Addressing the tribunal on the second day of hearings, Kohen said that the dispute over the archipelago of 700 islands in the south Atlantic – known in Argentina as the Malvinas – did not mean that the area was a “legal black hole” and that the UK could do as it wished with its natural resources.

“The fact that the parties dispute sovereignty does not turn the areas surrounding the Malvinas into some kind of Dominium maris Britannici,” he said. “We are not in the 17th century … We are in an era where we should put an end to the last vestiges of colonialism.”

Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, told the tribunal’s panel of judges on Tuesday that Argentina was seeking to further its sovereignty ambitions by applying for suspension of the drilling.

She claimed that such a move would kill the Sea Lion project, with “disastrous consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and the companies involved. The UK claimed that the tribunal, which adjudicates over maritime matters, does not have jurisdiction to wade into matters of sovereignty.

Kohen, switching from French to English, said the UK had failed to mention in its submissions the “elephant in the room” or the “whale in the bathtub”. The UN regarded the Falkland Islands as a non-self-governing territory, he said, and had called in 1976 for both sides to refrain from taking decisions that would unilaterally change the situation before the sovereignty dispute was settled.

The exploitation of hydrocarbons would put the islands among the “highest ranks of wealth just below the principality of Monaco” while depriving Argentina of its rights to those resources, Kohen told the tribunal.

Argentina’s legal team claimed that suspension of the drilling, which is due to start in March next year and which could double the GDP of the islands, was urgent given the irreparable damage to Argentina’s rights.
The UK has claimed there is no urgency as oil extraction would not take place until 2028, before which an Itlos arbitration panel would have come to a conclusion on the future of the oilfield.

In his closing remarks to the panel of 20 judges, Mario Oyarzábal, a legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said they rejected the UK’s attempt to characterise the proceedings as an attempt to litigate the sovereignty dispute.

He said: “The question before this tribunal is a much narrower one: whether, while the underlying dispute remains unresolved, the UK may unilaterally authorise or carry out new drilling for the exploitation of hydrocarbons in the disputed maritime area.”

Milei described the reclaiming of the Falklands as a “national cause” during his recent speech at the UN general assembly. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982 on the orders of the dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
The UK will offer further submissions on Wednesday.

articles.title: DepEd: Clean water, hygiene critical to nutrition
articles.summary: Access to safe drinking water and clean sanitation facilities is just as critical to a child’s nutrition and classroom performance as serving nutritious meals, the Department of Education…

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am
This file photo shows the Department of Education.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Access to safe drinking water and clean sanitation facilities is just as critical to a child’s nutrition and classroom performance as serving nutritious meals, the Department of Education (DepEd) emphasized during a global education and nutrition summit in Lusaka, Zambia.

At the Global Child Nutrition Forum 2026, DepEd, represented by Assistant Secretary for governance and operations Roger Masapol, shared the Philippines’ experience in institutionalizing its Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Schools (WinS) Program.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara underscored that healthy school environments are foundational to addressing learning gaps, noting that children struggle to process lessons or digest essential nutrients if they are frequently falling ill from preventable waterborne diseases.

“You cannot separate a child’s physical health from their ability to learn. Feeding programs work best when paired with clean water to drink, safe toilets to use and daily handwashing habits that keep kids healthy and in school,” Angara said.
Angara said sustained policy commitment, institutionalization, clear standards and systematic monitoring have transformed school health environments across the country.
“What we shared in Zambia is a decade of hard-earned progress, proving that when we invest in basic hygiene and sanitation, we are directly investing in our learners’ nutrition and future,” he added.
Tuition subsidy

Meanwhile, families with children enrolled in participating private junior high schools are set to receive bigger tuition subsidies after DepEd secured the first increase in Educational Service Contracting (ESC) grant rates since 2017.
Starting School Year 2027-2028, the approved rate adjustment will apply to incoming Grade 7 ESC grantees.
Under the new structure, annual ESC grants in the National Capital Region will rise from P13,000 to P17,500.
Grantees in highly urbanized cities outside Metro Manila will receive P14,500 from P11,000, while those in all other regions will receive P12,000, up from P9,000.

articles.title: ‘Don’t traumatize witness vs Duterte’
articles.summary: Lawyers representing drug war victims have asked the International Criminal Court to limit a witness’ time in court to “safeguard their psychological well-being.”

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am

In former president Rodrigo Duterte’s crimes against humanity case, common legal representatives of the victims are supporting the prosecution’s request to admit witness P-1303’s prior recorded testimony.
International Criminal Court
MANILA, Philippines — Lawyers representing drug war victims have asked the International Criminal Court (ICC) to limit a witness’ time in court to “safeguard their psychological well-being.”
P-1303 would testify on a drug-related killing, details of which were redacted.
“The time she is required to spend in court should be kept to a minimum, consistent with the requirements of a fair and equitable trial,” lawyers said.
“Reducing the number of times she is required to recall and relive these memories in the courtroom would help to significantly mitigate the psychological impact of giving testimony,” they added.
Introducing her prior recorded statement would reduce the duration of her oral testimony, they maintained.
If approved, the witness will still be presented for supplementary examination and cross-examination by the defense.
Lawyers Gilbert Andres, Joel Butuyan and Paolina Massidda signed the filing.

MANILA, Philippines — The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) has reminded government agencies to keep Christmas celebrations and year-end parties merry but modest as the country faces an energy emergency and a looming El Niño peak.

articles.title: Dynasties ‘more entrenched’ in House bill – Carpio
articles.summary: Political dynasties “will become more entrenched” if the proposed bill by the House of Representatives is approved, retired Supreme Court justice Antonio Carpio warned.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am
Retired Supreme Court justice Antonio Carpio warned.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Political dynasties “will become more entrenched” if the proposed bill by the House of Representatives is approved, retired Supreme Court justice Antonio Carpio warned.

In an interview over radio dzBB yesterday, Carpio again raised his objection to the House bill authored by Speaker Faustino Dy III and Majority Leader Sandro Marcos of Ilocos Norte’s first district, which proposes a ban on family members up to the second degree of ties from public office.
The bill was “divided into five categories,” with the president, vice president and senators in one category, and congressmen and local positions in separate categories, Carpio explained.
“The father can run for president, the nephew and niece for vice president, and the uncle and auntie for the Senate because that’s outside the second degree,” he pointed out.
Meanwhile, siblings belonging to a family of politicians may seek election in each legislative district in a province or in each town and city, he added.
Carpio maintained, “It will be worse, the political dynasties will be more entrenched.”

According to earlier reports, Dy and Marcos – who both belong to dynasties – proposed under House Bill 8389 that spouses and relatives within the second degree of consanguinity or affinity may be prohibited from simultaneously seeking or holding elective posts within the same political jurisdiction, such as a single province, city, municipality or barangay.

Deputy Speaker Francisco Paolo Ortega V, who belongs to the political dynasty in La Union, defended the measure, saying it was the “most realistic” and would balance the effort to control political power and the democratic right to vote leaders.

The Dapat Isa Lang Movement, of which Carpio is one of the convenors, had rejected the proposed House bill and maintained the ban on political dynasties should be extended to the fourth degree, or up to the first cousins, uncles and aunts, nephews and nieces, grandparents and grandchildren and others belonging to four generations of a public official and his or her spouse.
It has launched an online signature campaign wherein they proposed that only one member of the family within the fourth degree can run in each national and local position, according to Carpio.

The group has employed the people’s initiative, wherein they have to collect signatures of the constitutionally required three percent of the registered voters in each of the country’s 254 legislative districts or 10 percent of registered voters nationwide, to be able to advance its call for Congress to enact its proposed anti-dynasty law, he explained.
While the group has not set a deadline for the gathering of signatures, Carpio said they may gather signatures up to next year, ahead of the next presidential polls in 2028.

The Supreme Court in its landmark ruling last August has ordered Congress to pass an anti-dynasty law after 39 years that it has not been implemented despite being mandated by the Constitution, which was tantamount to grave abuse of discretion.

It also suggested that the ban on political dynasties could be applied up to the fourth degree “including half-blood, adoptive, step and common-law relationships, as well as both legitimate and illegitimate filiations.”

articles.title: LPG price rollback possible this month
articles.summary: Users of liquefied petroleum gas may get an early Christmas gift this month as large cuts in international prices could lead to a rollback in local LPG prices.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am
MANILA, Philippines — Users of liquefied petroleum gas may get an early Christmas gift this month as large cuts in international prices could lead to a rollback in local LPG prices.

Contract prices in global markets, as determined by Saudi oil giant Aramco, have plummeted by $90 per metric ton after the Democratic Party routed the Republican Party of US President Donald Trump in last week’s midterm elections, Regasco president Arnel Ty said yesterday.
If the price trend continues until the end of the month, LPG prices may fall in December by anywhere between P5 and P6 per kilo.
But Ty raised the possibility of implementing the rollback as early as this month, depending on what transpires in Thursday’s meeting between LPG players and the Department of Energy.
“Probably, because of this softening of prices, we might experience an advanced rollback for LPG,” Ty told “Money Talks” on One News.
“But we have to communicate first with the DOE that if any brand will have an advanced rollback, it should be credited as a rollback of December’s contract price,” he added.
Household cooking has become more expensive ever since the Middle East war broke out in late February.
Demand for LPG is down by as much as 30 percent this year, according to Ty, though he is confident that vendors could recover their losses.
“We believe we can recoup that once the international market price of LPG starts going down,” he said.
Motorists are enjoying lower crude prices, with the price of gasoline plunging this week by as much as P17 per liter and diesel by P4 per liter.

articles.title: Myanmar junta from ASEAN, Marcos urged
articles.summary: Opposition lawmakers have called on the Marcos administration to bar representatives of the Myanmar military junta from participating in the Philippines’ hosting of the Association of Southeast…

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am
President Bongbong Marcos
Frederic J. Brown / AFP

MANILA, Philippines — Opposition lawmakers have called on the Marcos administration to bar representatives of the Myanmar military junta from participating in the Philippines’ hosting of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit in Manila, which begins on Monday.

Through House Resolution 1614, Akbayan party-list lawmakers Reps. Chel Diokno, Percival Cendaña and Dadah Kiram Ismula, Mamamayang Liberal party-list Rep. Leila de Lima and Kaka Bag-ao of Dinagat Islands emphasized that Manila must lead the regional bloc in enforcing the Five-Point Consensus and in pushing for inclusive engagement that involves democratic representatives, civil society, ethnic organizations and women and youth leaders.
The Five-Point Consensus is a peace plan forged between ASEAN and Myanmar’s junta in April 2021 in response to the political and humanitarian crisis triggered by a military coup earlier in the year.
Ismula stressed that compromising on the diplomatic isolation of the junta would deal a severe blow to regional credibility and to the Philippines’ standing as ASEAN chair.
“As the chair of ASEAN, the Philippines carries a historic responsibility to uphold the democratic values and humanitarian principles that bind our region together,” Ismula said.

“It will be a moral failure of the Philippines if we allow our chairmanship to be used to legitimize a military junta that continues to brutalize its own people, slaughter civilians and trample upon basic human rights,” Ismula added.

She also highlighted that the crisis in Myanmar directly threatens Filipino citizens and regional security through sprawling cyber-enabled scam compounds, online trafficking networks and forced labor hubs linked to the junta.

articles.title: Philippines ready to welcome ASEAN leaders
articles.summary: The Philippines will welcome heads of state and government to Manila for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit and Related Summits from Nov. 15 to 17 as the 10-member bloc faces many…

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines —The Philippines will welcome heads of state and government to Manila for the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits from Nov. 15 to 17 as the 10-member bloc faces many challenges in the global environment.
The high-level engagements will commence on Nov. 15 with the opening ceremony at the Philippine International Convention Center (PICC).

It will be followed by the plenary and retreat sessions, where ASEAN leaders will take stock of the Philippines’ Chairship achievements and discuss ways to strengthen ASEAN’s collective capacity to address emerging regional and global challenges, including the situation in Myanmar.
The leaders will have interface meetings with ASEAN parliamentarians, the business community and the youth.
Joining President Marcos, who chairs this year’s summit are leaders from ASEAN member states Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Lao PDR, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam.
Myanmar will be represented by the Director-General of the ASEAN Affairs Department of its Foreign Ministry.
Meanwhile, ASEAN Secretary-General Kao Kim Hourn will lead the ASEAN Secretariat Delegation to participate in the ASEAN Summit and Related Summits.
The plenary will feature remarks from the leaders of Brazil and Canada as well as the International Monetary Fund as guests of the ASEAN Chair.

Related summits or the Plus One summits will commence on Nov. 16 and continue until Nov. 17. The engagements will provide an opportunity to reaffirm existing partnerships and advance cooperation on shared regional and global priorities with ASEAN’s dialogue partners Australia, China, India, Japan, New Zealand, Republic of Korea, Russia, United Nations, and the United States of America, whose leaders are joining President Marcos to co-chair the related summits. – Emmanuel Tupas, Andrew Ronquillo, Evelyn Macairan, Ric Sapnu

articles.title: Defense: Sara did not get double pay
articles.summary: After presenting the Davao City accountant as witness before the Senate impeachment court, Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team believes that it was able to disprove that she received…

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — After presenting the Davao City accountant as witness before the Senate impeachment court, Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team believes that it was able to disprove that she received double compensation in 2023.

Duterte spokesman Paolo Panelo said the defense yesterday managed to debunk claims by the House prosecution team that she received income from the Davao city government while serving as vice president.

Panelo cited alleged efforts by prosecutors to divert the issue after defense witness Davao City accountant Vingelin Bajan was grilled about her connection to an accounting firm and her trips to China.
“Because as senators-judges, although many of them are not lawyers, right? For me, they should know what is relevant to the matter and what is not,” Panelo said.

Upon cross-examination, the senators learned that Bajan remained a partner at the accounting firm Ampil, Elises, Ciudadano and Co. CPAs while she was already a Davao city hall employee, constituting conflict of interest.
The prosecution pointed out the link to cast doubt on her credibility as defense witness.

Panelo said Bajan presented documents showing that the 2023 payment to the Vice President covered salary differentials for 2020 and 2021, when she was still mayor, that had not been paid amid a delay in the completion of the documentary requirements.

“They should control themselves by asking only those questions that are relevant to the issue at hand. The only question, the simple question is, does VP Sara have any hidden wealth that was not declared in her SALN?” Panelo added.
According to Panelo, the amount paid by the Davao City LGU represented her salary differential.

“The city accountant of Davao City, she explained that this P60,000 to P80,000 paid to VP Sara in 2023 is not double compensation, but salary differential for income she should have earned as mayor in 2020 to 2021,” he said.
‘Loose investment’
A defense witness said GenCorp Industries Inc. paid Duterte at least P2,142,369.14 in “loose investment” from 2022 to 2025.
Defense counsel Justin Nicol Gular presented GenCorp and Metro City Chow Foods Corp. in-house counsel Suzette Balucanag-Punay, who testified that GenCorp issued a series of checks to Duterte.
“From the year 2022 to 2025, how much was the total disbursement from GenCorp Industries Inc. to Vice President Sara Zimmerman Duterte?” Gular asked Punay.
“It’s a total of 2,142,369 pesos and 14 centavos,” Punay said in her response.
Gular asked Punay regarding the disbursements from 2022 to 2025 to the Vice President.
“It’s a return of capital,” Punay added.

House prosecution witness financial forensic analyst accountant-lawyer Alexander Cabrera had said Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio had unexplained wealth amounting to at least P1.5 billion based on voluminous bank, tax and other government records.
“Compared to what you said and the figures shown in the forensic report of Atty. Alex Cabrera, how do you describe the difference?” Gular asked.
“Very big difference, sir,” Punay replied to Gular.
Gular noted that based on the supposed forensic report of Cabrera, the alleged total computed undeclared income of Duterte from GenCorp in 2023 was P55,714,292.
Punay said that in 2023, GenCorp paid Duterte P555,750, representing her “return of capital.”
According to Punay, GenCorp disbursed P612,419.14 and P636,700 to Duterte in 2024 and 2025, respectively.
Gular noted that Cabrera claimed that Duterte’s undeclared income in 2024 was P74,056,480 and in 2025, it was P82,858,946.
Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero asked Punay what was the purpose of the payments made by GenCorp to Duterte.

“Why is GenCorp giving a monthly amount to the Vice President from the Times Square branch from June 2022, presumably when the branch was open. And then nothing from January to April in 2024, but monthly for the years 2023 and 2025. You characterized it as return on capital,” Escudero asked Punay.
“The return of capital was from the loose investment, which was carried over to Great Jolly Times, Times Square B and eventually to GenCorp,” Punay said.
She confirmed that Duterte owned 20 percent of Metro City Chow Foods Corp., with P50,000 subscribed capital and P12,500 paid-up capital.
While Duterte was a member of the board of directors and the compensation committee from 2022 to 2025, she did not participate in board meetings or transactions, Punay said.
Financial interest

“My interpretation of the constitutional prohibition you’re referring to is that you are not prohibited from having a financial interest in a private business. What is prohibited is that you actively manage and participate in a private business,” Panelo said.

“So, if you have an investment in a corporation and you receive passive dividends or compensation from that investment, that is not prohibited. My other example, besides former president Cory Aquino, is former vice president Leni Robredo when she was vice president, she declared shares of stocks in Meralco and Rockwell Land, if I’m not mistaken. So, if it declared a dividend, Vice President Leni received it during those times. And that is not forbidden,” Panelo added.
The defense team has withdrawn 15 bank officials from its initial list of 24 witnesses, except for BPI lawyer Paul Roderick Ysmael who will face the court today.

articles.title: Adjusted mall hours start next week
articles.summary: Mall operators in the capital will adjust operating hours to ease holiday traffic, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) said yesterday.

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am
From Nov. 16 to Dec. 25, malls are open from 11 a.m. to 11 p.m. on weekdays.
BY-NC-ND / Jurgen Proschinger / Mall
MANILA, Philippines —Mall operators in the capital will adjust operating hours to ease holiday traffic, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority (MMDA) said yesterday.
The adjusted mall hours will not take effect on holidays.
Mall deliveries will be limited from 11 p.m. to 5 a.m., MMDA Chairman Romando Artes said.
“Nighttime delivery will only be allowed. Perishable goods will be allowed during regular time,” he noted.
Ayala Malls, SM Malls, Ortigas Land, Robinsons Land, Araneta City, The Podium, Lucky Chinatown and other shopping mall operators made the agreement, he said.
Mall-wide sales will not be allowed except on weekends, the MMDA said.
“Individual outlets within malls may conduct sales on weekdays, provided that no announcements, advertisements or tarpaulins are made to promote them,” the agency added.
Mall operators are required to submit a traffic management plan to the MMDA two weeks before mall sales or promotional events, Artes said.
Restaurants, supermarkets and government services within mall premises will not be included in the extended operating hours.
Cinemas may operate at an earlier time on Dec. 25 to accommodate film audiences.

articles.title: Witness: VP got P2.14 million ‘return of capital’ from GenCorp
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte received a total of P2.14 million as “return of capital” from 2022 to 2025 from GenCorp Industries Inc., a corporation tied to her and her husband, its legal…

blocks.text: November 12, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Vice President Sara Duterte received a total of P2.14 million as “return of capital” from 2022 to 2025 from GenCorp Industries Inc., a corporation tied to her and her husband, its legal counsel said at the resumption of her impeachment trial yesterday.
Suzette Balucanag-Punay, GenCorp and Metro City Chow Foods’ in-house counsel, told the impeachment court that Duterte received the amount as “return of capital” through bank checks from GenCorp.
Punay earlier told the court that GenCorp gave Duterte P337,500 in 2022, P555,750 in 2023, P612,419 in 2024 and P636,700 in 2025, when she was already Vice President.

Questioning Punay, Sen. Risa Hontiveros said, “The loose investment started in 2007. But in 2022, 2023, 2024, at 2025, the Vice President earned a total of P2.14 million from what you call ‘return of capital,’ right?” Punay replied in the affirmative.

Hontiveros then maintained that based on documents submitted to the court, the money the Vice President received in the years covered by the disbursements were not mere “return of capital” or payouts for “loose investments.”

During her testimony, Punay and defense counsels used the term “loose investment” repeatedly and although not an official financial term, they explained that this represented undocumented contributions by Duterte to Jollibee Times Square branch in Davao City.

With Punay confirming that Duterte had profited from the setup, Hontiveros emphasized that corporate payouts such as those received by Duterte in those years violated the 1987 Constitution, which strictly mandates that the Vice President “cannot directly or indirectly … participate in any business.”

Asked whether the Vice President violated the Constitution with her business interests, Punay initially replied she was “not sure,” but later backtracked when reminded of specific provisions in the Constitution.
Sen. Francis Pangilinan then pointed out that it was incorrect for Punay to testify that the Vice President had no position or participation in any of GenCorp businesses.
“But receiving benefits, you are a recipient, then you have a role, a beneficiary of GenCorp. So it’s not correct to say that there is no participation or no role whatsoever,” he said.

“Let’s be clear here. You said – you were so categorical, you were so clear that there’s no participation whatsoever. And now it’s turning out, there is one – as a recipient,” Pangilinan said. “As a recipient, yes,” Punay added.
Admission

Hontiveros also argued that the Vice President had already declared in her statement of assets, liabilities and net worth (SALN) that she had business interests in GenCorp from 2024 to 2025 and it would be incorrect for her counsels to claim that she had no business interests in the company.
“She made an admission already,” Hontiveros said.
Sen. Panfilo Lacson said Duterte’s own notarized wealth declaration carries heavier evidentiary weight than standard corporate records.
Lacson raised the matter during debates wherein the prosecution pressed Punay on whether Duterte has financial ties to Jollibee franchises owned by GenCorp.

In her SALN, Duterte listed herself as a shareholder of GenCorp but Punay – testifying for the defense – said the Vice President was not an actual stockholder because her “unilateral declaration” in the SALN does not make her a stockholder.

This prompted Lacson to ask the witness which document holds more probative weight – a notarized document like SALN or a General Information Sheet (GIS) issued by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
“As far as I know, an admission against interest has greater probative weight or admissibility weight than GIS,” he said.
“I know somebody who got jailed for an admission made on TV. This SALN is notarized,” Lacson said, apparently referring to Sen. Rodante Marcoleta, who is in detention for plunder.

Defense counsel Justin Gular manifested that an “admission against interest” is merely an exception to the hearsay rule, not a rule for determining the probative weight of evidence, adding that such weighing is solely the prerogative of the senator-judges.
Prosecution counsel Lorna Kapunan quickly rebutted the defense, quoting Section 27 of the Rules of Court on testimonial evidence to assert that an admission is the highest form of evidence.

“Not only is (the SALN) a public document, if we weigh two public documents, the General Information Sheet that is certified by the corporate secretary and not by the VP, compared to a SALN that is certified to and sworn to personally by the VP herself... a public document personally sworn and subscribed to by the person – the VP herself – carries higher weight,” Kapunan argued.
‘Mind your preposition’
Presiding officer Francis Escudero acknowledged that both counsels’ arguments were correct, but reminded them that it is the senator-judges who would decide on the conflicting documents.
Escudero earlier during the hearing sought to clarify from the defense witness if what she meant was “return on capital” and not “return of capital.”
For Escudero, P2.14-million earnings from a Jollibee branch represented not merely a return of her P46,875 investment.
“Please take note of the preposition. This is not return of investment. This is return on investment, the capital earned already,” Escudero said.
Sen. Raffy Tulfo castigated the witness for either feigning ignorance or being incompetent in her testimony on Duterte’s business interests in GenCorp.

“You should have at least asked from GenCorp a copy of the canceled check so you would be ready here. It seems to me that 15 years as a lawyer, you’re still not prepared – or just feigning ignorance,” he said.
Sen. Erwin Tulfo flagged Duterte’s “conflict of interest,” citing GenCorp’s P1-billion sales from 2022 to 2024 when Duterte was already Vice President, up from P28 million in 2021.

Punay said that with GenCorp’s five Jollibee branches, “it follows that the income would increase.” But she said she has no personal knowledge of the earnings hike because she is not part of operations.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian confronted the witness about the Vice President’s apparent conflict of interest in GenCorp., citing the firm’s 19 contracts with the Davao City government where her brother Sebastian Duterte is the incumbent mayor.
Sen. Imee Marcos explained the Vice President’s P2.14-million “return of capital.”

“If you returned what was borrowed, the original principal amount is being restored, and it’s like paid-in capital or equity or refinancing. And when the corporation is sold, it becomes part of sales proceeds,” Marcos said. – Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Delon Porcalla

articles.title: Is the US blue wave a turning point for Europe, too?
articles.summary:
Far-right populists remain insurgent and pro-EU governments are braced for Trump’s betrayal. But the midterms also showed that democracy can fight back

•

blocks.text: “Is Maga dead?” asked Margaret, a Guardian reader in Switzerland, in a live Q&A with our correspondents after the seismic US midterm elections. If Margaret’s query expressed a hope that the Democrats’ blue wave could transform Europe’s fortunes after two years of Maga-induced trauma, she was probably not alone.

The resounding defeat for Donald Trump’s Republicans and the installation of a Democratic-controlled US Congress has been met with understandable relief in European capitals. In the short term however, the worst for Europe is not over. Trump didn’t need congressional approval, after all, to unleash a trade war on his supposed European allies, threaten to invade Greenland, try to stitch up Ukraine or go to war with Iran, an act that has inflated fuel and food prices disastrously.

Hemmed in now on domestic policy, the US president may, many European leaders fear, use his extensive foreign policy powers to become even more confrontational on the world stage. Europe, warned Nathalie Tocci, is exactly where Trump will lash out. “Trump and Maga have always seen Europe as the mirror image of their domestic foes: a bunch of presumptuous, woke, emasculated liberals. Now that those foes have made a comeback at home, Trump’s rancour towards Europe is likely to grow.”

The lashing out could come in the form of new tariff chaos. As the humiliated Maga figurehead (one Washington expert likened the movement now to “a cornered ferret”), Trump could veto aid for Ukraine and thwart Kyiv’s access to defence technology. Paul Taylor sketched a fearful scenario in which he could even attempt a carve-up of eastern Europe in the so-called “big, beautiful deal” for Ukraine that he says he is working on with Russia. The omens for Europe were poor as US-mediated talks opened in Abu Dhabi, with delegates from Germany, France, the UK and the EU, literally sidelined.

Nor can Europe rely on the new intake of congressional Democrats to challenge Trump on its behalf, Blanche Leridon of the Institut Montaigne thinktank in Paris, tells me. “We have to be clear-sighted that the Democrats’ priority in Congress won’t be to re-establish a more harmonious relationship with Europe. Their foreign policy is, at this point, difficult to decipher. There isn’t a single, consistent position between the more progressive and centrist factions when it comes to either Europe or Ukraine specifically.”

We can’t even assume that nationalist populist parties, encouraged by Trump to destroy the EU from the inside, will suffer by their association with him. True, in central and eastern Europe, where the Maga spirit was heavily promoted by Viktor Orbán, some incumbents may have to perform a pivot. Poland’s conservative president Karol Nawrocki, who is backed by the opposition Eurosceptic Law and Justice party and has vaunted his proximity to Trump, is now facing awkward questions. And in Czechia, which has one of the most pro-Maga governments in Europe, populist PM Andrej Babiš and his far-right coalition partners, the Motorists party, have faced a wave of grassroots protests lately.
In Italy meanwhile, the far-right prime minister Giorgia Meloni played up tensions with Trump months ago, a strategic move to allay the concerns of voters, the majority of whom despise him.

But in countries where populists have not yet been in government and are polling at record levels, Trump’s humiliation may not matter to voters, even if their grievances – such as stagnant pay, inflation and lack of affordable housing – are often driven by global forces.

“It would be wrong to conclude that national-populist and reactionary forces are in retreat everywhere in the west,” Leridon says. “The Democrats won in the US because people were fed up with Trump, in Serbia, [Aleksandar] Vučić was overthrown after 14 years, but in countries where populist political forces are not in power, but on the verge of gaining it, the calculation is different.”

In France, Marine Le Pen is still leading in the polls, six months ahead of a presidential election being fought on cost-of-living issues. Her far-right National Rally party identified Trump as a liability some time ago. “Le Pen and [Jordan] Bardella understood perfectly the radioactive effect the US president could have on them as politicians claiming to defend French national interests. Above all, they recoiled from the corrosive impact of Trump’s policies on purchasing power in France, whether via trade tariffs or the war in Iran,” Leridon says.

In Germany, Alice Weidel, a co-leader of the far-right Alternative für Deutschland, had also distanced the party from Trump in response to tariffs and Greenland. Weidel now blames Trump’s defeat on broken promises about going to war with Iran.

A critical test for Europe’s political direction is looming in Spain. Socialist prime minister Pedro Sánchez, who called a snap election for 29 November, welcomed Trump’s defeat as a straw in the wind for the revival of progressive forces. But amid public outcry over housing and wages (the cause of Wednesday’s general strike), the momentum is with the opposition rightwing Popular Party (PP) – which could coalesce with the far-right Vox. If this happens, it will be the first time a far-right party enters government in Spain since the end of the Franco dictatorship in 1975. Santiago Abascal, the Vox leader, dismissed any suggestion of an ideological connection with Trump’s Republicans. “We are in Spain, not in Michigan,” he said after the midterms.
after newsletter promotion
A yearning for generational change

blocks.caption: The youth movement in Serbia toppled a government. Photograph: Uros Arsic/Reuters

blocks.text: And yet, longer term, the broader, more hopeful lesson from across the Atlantic could be that after years of global backsliding liberal democracy is not dead. “If Europe can celebrate an essential point, it is that American democracy is alive and was the big winner of these elections,” Leridon says.

Could this even, as Alexander Hurst asked, be a “democratic spring” – one that began in Budapest in April with Orbán’s defeat? Julian Borger unpacked how a sequence of four pivotal elections this year, in Hungary, Serbia, Brazil and now the US, has shown the power of grassroots activism to produce surprises and could, perhaps, begin the reversal of a worldwide drift towards authoritarianism.

The US vote could even shake Europe’s ailing mainstream parties out of their fatalistic mimicking of far-right policies and into action. Gen Z voters fuelled the US blue wave, which showed a yearning for generational change. At a time when youth-led protest movements have rocked Europe, progressive parties may be able to channel protest energy into serious political change. They can’t say they haven’t been warned, loudly, to heed calls for democratic renewal, education, decent housing, equality and limits on the power of the big tech billionaires. Or that failure to do so could allow grassroots anger to be co-opted into the same kind of anti-system nihilism that fuelled Maga.

articles.title: EXPLAINER: Why are more Filipino youths facing unemployment challenges
articles.summary: The unemployment rate in the Philippines climbed to 5.4% in September 2026 from 3.5% in September 2025 -- the latest figure is equal to 2.86 million jobless people, according to the Philippine…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 11:24pm

The unemployment rate in the Philippines climbed to 5.4% in September 2026 from 3.5% in September 2025 — the latest figure is equal to 2.86 million jobless people, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA).
With this, the labor force, or people who are qualified to work, has also increased. However, not everyone is able to find work, according to a report from GMA News Feed.
Data from the PSA showed that there were 1.12 million youths unemployed in September 2026, which rose from the 741,000 recorded in the same time last year.
A Philippine Institute for Development Studies (PIDS) study showed that the curricula is not aligned with the training programs that would address the shifting needs of the industry.

There is also no national framework to determine middle skills, so the Technical Education and Skills Development Authority (TESDA), Commission on Higher Education (CHED) have different classifications.
Job creation
According to IBON Foundation executive director Sonny Africa, however, this went beyond a matter of skill mismatch.

“Ang pinakamalaking dahilan doon sa mataas na youth unemployment ay because hindi nakakapaglikha ng sapat na trabaho ‘yung agrikultura at industriya… Alam ko mahilig ‘yung gobyerno doon sa job creation, supposedly doon sa mga jobs fair. Kinokonek lang niya ‘yung mga naghahanap ng trabaho doon sa mga handang magtrabaho. So, hindi siya nagki-create ng trabaho, kundi kinokonek lang niya ‘yung supply at demand,” Africa said.

(The biggest reason for youth unemployment is there are no jobs being created in agriculture and industry… I know the government likes job creation supposedly in job fairs. But it only connects those who are looking for workers to those ready to work. So it does not create jobs, it connects supply and demand.)
Underemployed
The PSA also recorded 5.56 million underemployed Filipinos, or workers with a job but have expressed the need for additional work hours or a second job.
Africa said it is not enough to just create jobs now either. The government needs to ensure proper wages and benefits for workers.
The PIDS said there needs to be better coordination between TESDA, CHED, PSA and industry players to have streamlined standards and training programs.
The Labor Department has earlier stated that they will work to improve youth employment by working with employers, including local government units and others.

“For the Department of Labor and Employment, employment gains reflect continued labor market activity, particularly in the Services sector. However, the need to address the increase in unemployment also emphasizes the need to ensure that more Filipinos gain access to decent and sustainable employment opportunities,” DOLE said in a statement. — BAP, GMA News
