articles.title: Brazil electoral court fines Meta, sees no deliberate election bias
articles.summary: The fine came after President Lula's coalition filed a complaint. The court said there was no evidence of intent to influence the election. Meta said it will defend itself against "false allegations."

image.caption: The fine was based on Meta's overall handling of the court ordersImage: Thibault Camus/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Brazil's top electoral court has ordered Meta to pay 7.5 million reais ($1.34 million; €1.22 million) for failing to fully comply with judicial orders during last month's presidential election.
However, the judicial body has so far found no evidence that Meta deliberately acted to influence the election outcome.

Ahead of the runoff vote on October 25, leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's coalition filed a complaint, accusing Meta of "algorithmic manipulation" favoring his far-right rivalFlavio Bolsonaro.
Platforms owned by Meta include Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
Meta told the court last month that it had implemented measures to guarantee equal treatment for both campaigns.
Meta lacked transparency, court says
The Superior Electoral Court (TSE) unanimously ruled on Tuesday to impose the 7.5 million reais fine on the US tech giant.
Meta missed deadlines and lacked transparency in its investigation, the court said.

On the other hand, the court's reporting judge Marco Aurelio Belizze wrote in his ruling that there were no preliminary evidence indicating that any intentional actions were taken to influence the election.
"That ​conclusion would require robust evidence, to be produced through the appropriate legal proceedings," he said.

blocks.caption: In his victory speech, Lula reiterated that Brazil would "not accept being anyone’s backyard," a recurring campaign message defending the country’s sovereignty against US influenceImage: Natacha Pisarenko/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: According to Bellizze, the fine was based on Meta's overall handling of the court orders, including delays, incomplete disclosures, and challenges in verifying some of the information it provided.
In a statement on Wednesday, Meta strongly denied the court's ruling.
"We will continue to present the facts and defend ourselves against false allegations in the ‌ongoing ​legal proceedings," Meta said in a statement on Wednesday.
Lula vows to rein in social media
Lula defeated Bolsonaro in a tight run-off in October 25 with him winning 51.7% of the vote against Bolsonaro's 48.2%.
In his victory speech, Lula urged more regulation of big tech platforms after allegations that Meta interfered in the race.
"We had to overcome foreign interference in the election, coming from outside through digital platforms that we will have to regulate," he said.

articles.title: David Walliams cameo cut from Australian film after sexual harassment allegations
articles.summary: Children’s author and comedian, who wrote the book on which the movie Fing! is based, will also be removed from the publicity tour

blocks.text: The distributors of an upcoming Australian film based on a book by children’s author and television personality David Walliams have confirmed he will be removed from the film and its publicity run after sexual harassment allegations were made public.

Transmission Films has confirmed that Walliams, a co-writer of the children’s fantasy film Fing!, will no longer appear in the movie or take part in its media campaign before its 14 January cinema debut.
“Walliams will not be participating in the Australian publicity campaign. The campaign will focus on the film’s Australian production, director and lead cast,” Transmission Films said in a statement.
“The film’s producers have advised that they have removed Walliams’ cameo appearance from Fing!”

The decision comes after a joint investigation by the Guardian UK and ITV News revealed sexual harassment allegations, including allegations that Walliams groomed fans he met when they were as young as 15, and allegations he harassed women in the workplace over a number of years. He has denied the allegations.

The 55-year-old multimillionaire and Order of the British empire (OBE) recipient is one of the UK’s most famous comedians and writers. Earlier this year, his lawyers took a case to the high court in an attempt to stop the allegations from being published. The case was dismissed.

The film, based on the British writer’s 2019 book, was produced by Walliams’ production company, King Bert. It stars Taika Waititi, Mia Wasikowska, Iona Bell and Blake Harrison, and is directed by Australian film-maker Jeffrey Walker. Walliams co-wrote the screenplay with Kevin Cecil.
The streaming service Stan, which was eventually expected to host the film on its platform after its cinema release, has confirmed it will no longer stream the movie.
“In light of the recent and serious allegations against David Walliams, Stan has removed Fing! from its content slate,” a spokesperson said in a statement.

The film’s US distributor, Angel Studios, has also confirmed they have removed Walliams’s cameo, and he would also be cut from its US marketing materials, following the sexual misconduct allegations, which he denies.

“We take the allegations reported regarding David Walliams seriously,” they said in a statement to Variety. “Our thoughts are with anyone who has been affected. We have removed his cameo appearance from ‘Fing!,’ and he will have no involvement in the film’s release or promotion.”
The film’s UK-Ireland distributor, Sky, has confirmed it will completely abandon the film.

A Sky spokesperson said: “The allegations made against David Walliams are extremely serious. We have notified the producers of the film of our intention to exit our position as the UK & Ireland licensee of Fing!. We have already removed content which features him from our platforms.”
The film could still be shown elsewhere in the world, although it is not yet clear if the other actors and creatives involved will all wish it to be screened.

articles.title: Is AIIB's complaint mechanism failing affected communities?
articles.summary: The AIIB has a grievance redress mechanism for people affected by projects it finances. But those seeking to file a complaint face significant hurdles. Critics say reforms and greater transparency…

image.caption: The AIIB finances major infrastructure projects across AsiaImage: Noushad Variyattiyakkal/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: For members of the Indigenous Sasak community on the Indonesian island of Lombok, the conflict over their land is not over.

For them, a tourism and infrastructure project co-financed by the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB) is a source of frustration, as they believe it has led to the expropriation of their land and destruction of their livelihoods.
In late September, they officially filed a complaint with the bank. It remains unclear whether this complaint will lead to an independent investigation.
The AIIB, which finances major infrastructure projects across Asia, has a mechanism in place to deal with such complaints.
Individuals who suffer adverse effects from the bank-financed projects may, under certain conditions, file a complaint with the institution.
However, access to this process — known as the Project Complaints Mechanism (PPM) — remains controversial.

According to a report by The Diplomat, a magazine that covers political and economic developments in Asia, none of the 45 complaints listed on the AIIB's website had been deemed admissible as of mid-September.
The bank acknowledged that "no cases have passed the PPM's eligibility assessment," but it stressed that it is "only part of the story."
South Asia projects boost China's presence in India's sphere
Call for easier access
The AIIB emphasized that not every issue needs to be resolved through this mechanism.
The PPM is "only one part of AIIB's grievance redress ecosystem," the Beijing-based bank said in response to a query from DW.
Those affected should first attempt to resolve concerns directly with the project team at the local level, it said.
According to the bank, "twelve complaints were in fact resolved at the project level — as a direct result of AIIB's follow-up and intervention — and one was resolved through domestic courts."
But critics see this as a major weakness.
"The mechanism must be easily accessible," said Arntraud Hartmann, a development economist at the Johns Hopkins University School of Advanced International Studies (SAIS Europe) in Bologna, Italy.

She argued that people affected by the projects, for instance, are required to document potential violations of environmental and social standards from the start. "How is the affected party supposed to know which standards might have been violated?" she questioned.

The AIIB disputes this claim. "In terms of accessibility, we have made the submission form simpler and translated it into 12 languages," it said, adding that complaints can be submitted online, by phone, or by email.
Urgewald, a German environmental NGO, cites another problem with AIIB-financed projects.
For many of them, information on environmental impacts and resettlements is either missing or published late, it noted.

For 2024, the NGO found that 11 of the 16 projects it examined lacked complete environmental and social impact assessments. In many cases, information on the potential number of displaced residents was also missing, it added.

"The information published on the bank's website is often insufficient and inconsistent. Particularly important documents, such as environmental impact assessments or resettlement plans, vary widely or are missing entirely," said Nora Sausmikat, a China expert at Urgewald.

The lack of information makes it difficult for those affected to respond in a timely manner and report violations early on, she underscored, adding that the situation is particularly difficult for people without formal land titles.
China's plan to dominate the seas
'It's not enough'
Christoph Steinert, a political scientist at the University of Konstanz, said the mere existence of such grievance redressal mechanisms "is not enough."
Particularly vulnerable groups often know little about their rights, he said, adding that information should be available in local languages and targeted outreach directed at affected communities.
Criticism of the AIIB's procedures is not new.

A 2023 report by international aid organizations, including Recourse, Accountability Counsel, and Inclusive Development International, revealed that the AIIB's grievance mechanism had failed to accept a single complaint since its 2019 inception.
The study highlighted that 101 of the 219 AIIB-financed projects, or 46% of of the total projects at the time, were ineligible for review due to co-financing exemptions.

The AIIB typically provides funding without leading projects, a standard practice in development finance. When complaints arise, it directs complainants to the lead lender. As a result, nine of the 45 complaints fell outside its jurisdiction.
For Sausmikat, this is part of the problem. "The AIIB, however, decided against revising this requirement and established a mechanism that is very difficult to access," she said.

As of January 1, 2026, following two years of external consultations, the AIIB reformed its complaints mechanism. Under certain conditions, complaints can now be filed even while legal proceedings are ongoing.

But Sausmikat stressed that the changes are insufficient. Of the eight key recommendations made by an independent expert, only three were adopted, she underlined. "The revision did not remove the actual obstacles."
The AIIB stated that the reforms are intended to make the mechanism "more accessible and responsive."
The new rules have been in effect for only ten months, and their implementation is being closely monitored, the bank said.
China's plan to never run out of food
Fear of reprisals?
Steinert said fear of reprisals poses another fundamental challenge to such procedures.
Documented cases from Latin America, for instance, show that complainants have faced administrative or legal problems, and in some cases even violence.
Such risks could deter others from filing complaints, Steinert said.
However, his research does not specifically address AIIB projects.
The bank said that it "does not tolerate retaliation against anyone who raises concerns."
"Requestors may ask for confidentiality, and the revised PPM policy strengthens protection against reprisals," it added.
Sausmikat said Germany — as a co-founder and the fourth-largest shareholder of the AIIB — could also play a role, working with other member states to push for changes.

Hartmann also stressed that the bank's shareholders bear responsibility and urged the AIIB's Board of Directors to amend the rules governing the grievance mechanism. "We need a policy based on good-practice standards."
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.summary: Talks in Abu Dhabi centred around Europe's security framework, with US envoys due to meet Putin and Zelensky on Thursday.

blocks.text: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.
Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.
Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."

"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.
Both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.

After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
This latest round of talks had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.
For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.
For Moscow, it is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.

Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.

Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.

Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.

There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.

Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.

Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas.

This matter was the "hardest", Kushner acknowledged, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.

"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

articles.summary: The defense team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has dropped most of its bank representative witnesses, retaining only a representative from the Bank of the Philippine Islands…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 11:03pm

The defense team in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte has dropped most of its bank representative witnesses, retaining only a representative from the Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), in a bid to shorten the proceedings, spokesperson Michael Poa said.

Poa said the defense decided against calling the other bank representatives to avoid wasting the time of the Senate impeachment court and the witnesses, noting that testimonies on the authentication of bank records were already on record.

“We don’t think that there’s a need to, siguro, waste the time of the court… and waste the time also of the bank representatives sa pagpapatawag sa kanila tomorrow. Binawasan na natin, iniwan na lang natin yung sa BPI representative,” Poa said.
“We dropped, basically, the bank representatives,” he added.
Poa said dropping the witnesses would help abbreviate the proceedings. The defense also dropped a barangay captain from its witness list.
The spokesperson, however, did not disclose the identities of the remaining defense witnesses.

Earlier in the day at the trial, some senator-judges raised concerns about the lack of details in the testimony of GenCorp Industries and Metro City Chow Foods in-house lawyer Suzette Balucanag-Punay.

Asked about how the defense planned to address these gaps, Poa said that there will be other witnesses to be presented who could answer questions about Duterte’s Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

“I don’t think there’s a hierarchy of gaps or anything like that but with the questions of the senator-judges, for example, ‘Why is it in the SALN’, ‘Why do the SEC [Securities and Exchange Commission] documents reflect otherwise’, those are the issues we will address with future witnesses,” Poa said in a mix of English and Filipino.—Jean Mangaluz/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Wael Mohya could make German football history at 17
articles.summary: At just 17, Gladbach forward Wael Mohya has earned his first Germany call-up. The dual-national talent has chosen the DFB path for now — and could soon make modern national-team history.

image.caption: Wael Mohya has the chance to make German football history if he plays under Jürgen KloppImage: Marvin Ibo Güngör/GES/picture alliance

blocks.text: If you watch the Bundesliga, then you'll know Wael Mohya is a fast-footed, quick-thinking footballer. But not even the 17-year-old (Mohya turns 18 on December 31) Borussia Mönchengladbach youngster would have expected to be called up to the Germany squad so soon.
"Of course, I was absolutely thrilled. It means a great, great deal to me. I think everyone dreams of being selected for the national team at some point," Mohya said.
"And the fact that it's come to this now is, of course, just awesome and makes me very proud."
Mohya was at the gym when the call came in. He then shared the good news with his parents over dinner. "They started crying," the teenager said in a video posted on Gladbach's social media channels.

The youngster, who was born in a small town east of Düsseldorf, smiles and laughs a lot in interviews. He is always friendly, and in a good mood. On the field, too, he exudes the lightheartedness and carefree spirit of a 17-year-old.

As a technically skilled and creative player, Mohya often seeks out one-on-one situations and puts his opponents under pressure with quick dribbles. In nine Bundesliga appearances this season, Mohya has scored twice and delivered one assist.
"He's so cool and just plays really well. It's fun to watch him," Borussia coach Alexander Blessin said recently.

"Wael brings a lot to the team with his laid-back attitude on the field. He's not afraid to take risks, no matter how much pressure there is," added Gladbach's sporting director Rouven Schröder on a talk show on Sport1.
Wael 'Waffel' Mohya working on and off the pitch

Borussia Mönchengladbach has been Mohya's sporting home since he was seven years old. Last season, previous head coach Eugen Polanski promoted him to the first team, and in December 2025, Mohya made his Bundesliga debut. Against Wolfsburg, aged 16 years and 347 days old, he became the youngest Bundesliga player in the club's history.

Mohya also recently completed a voluntary social year at an elementary school in Mönchengladbach. This is a program in Germany for young people who volunteer in social sectors—such as hospitals, schools, or nursing homes—for about six to 18 months. They gain work experience, help others, and earn a little money.

At the school's open all-day care program, Mohya helped serve meals, assisted children with their homework, and played with them. That's also where his nickname comes from. Because a girl hadn't understood his first name correctly or couldn't pronounce it, she called him "Waffel." Now, that name has stuck.

blocks.caption: Wael Mohya made his debut against Wolfsburg in late 2025Image: Maximilian Koch/picture alliance

blocks.text: Many clubs interested in Mohya

Even before being called up to the Germany team, clubs in the Bundesliga and across Europe's top leagues had taken notice of Mohya and were trying to sign him. His contract with Borussia Mönchengladbach runs through 2028.

With Gladbach currently in a relegation battle, his future appears likely to be elsewhere. If the club wants to generate transfer revenue from its biggest talent, next summer would likely be the opportunity to sell him—unless he extends his contract with Borussia.

The 17-year-old's career is managed by his parents. Whichever club can convince them that their son is in good hands and help him reach his full potential likely has the best chance of securing Mohya's signing.
Mohya himself says he doesn't even know how much he's currently earning at Gladbach.
"My parents take care of all that," he told Bild recently. "I get a monthly allowance, which is more than enough for me."
Germany head coach Jürgen Klopp recently revealed how much he had enjoyed his conversations with the youngster.
"The conversations I had with him were great," Klopp said with a laugh. "I wasn't that confident at 17, but then again, I wasn't that good either."
Decision in favor of Germany over Morocco

Since Mohya's parents are from Morocco, their son also holds Moroccan citizenship. As a result, he could have played for Morocco, but he has now decided against it. In fact, the Moroccan football association had been actively courting Mohya as early as last year and had already reached out to him in the run-up to the 2026 World Cup.

Now, like Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib, Mohya will continue to play in the German jersey, unlike Schalke's Soufiane El-Faouzi, who chose Morocco, or Bayer Leverkusen's Ibrahim Maza, who likely would have been selected by Klopp as well if he hadn't already opted for Algeria.

For Mohya, who played for Germany's youth teams from the U16s through to the U21s, the door to Morocco remains open only as long as he hasn't yet played a competitive match for Germany. If Mohya plays in the upcoming UEFA Nations League games in Serbia or against the Netherlands, another record is on the horizon. Although there were two even younger players who made their debuts in the Germany jersey—Willy Baumgärtner in 1908 (at 17 years and 104 days) and Marius Hiller in 1910 (at 17 years and 241 days)—the era in which they debuted is hardly comparable. And so, while Wael Mohya would rank third overall on the list, he would become the youngest Germany player in the modern era. The youngest to date was Hamburg legend Uwe Seeler in 1954, aged 17 years and 345 days.
This article was adapted from German.

articles.title: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
articles.summary: Leonardo Bertulazzi, a former member of the Marxist guerrilla group the Red Brigades, was about to be extradited to his home country of Italy.

blocks.text: A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.
Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.

His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.
Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.
He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.
Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.
When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.

Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.
However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.
A nationwide manhunt is now under way.
Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.
Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.
However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.
Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".
He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.
Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.

The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.

Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 42: Loose investment, conflict of interest raised
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte"s loose investment in GenCorp Industries Inc., which earned her P2.14 million in income despite not being listed as the firm"s shareholder in corporate records, took…

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 10:42pm

Vice President Sara Duterte’s loose investment in GenCorp Industries Inc., which earned her P2.14 million in income despite not being listed as the firm’s shareholder in corporate records, took center stage during Day 42 of her impeachment trial.

Lawyer Suzette Balucanag-Punay, in-house counsel of GenCorp and Metro City Chow Foods Corp., testified that this loose interest stemmed from the investment she made in Davao Bounty Times Corporation, an entity that was supposed to operate the Jollibee Times Square branch in Davao City.
Punay, however, said the subject Jollibee branch was not granted a franchise and that it opened under Great Jolly Times Food Corp., which eventually became GenCorp.

Punay’s testimony, however, did not explain why GenCorp was paying out the Vice President for her return of capital worth over P2 million from 2022 to 2025 when her investment was made to Davao Bounty Times Corporation.
Impeachment court presiding officer Senator Francis Escudero told Punay they will issue a subpoena for additional documents that would justify the legality of GenCorp’s payout to the Vice President.

Ahead of disclosing Duterte's loose interest in GenCorp, Punay said that the Vice President is not a stockholder of the company, one of her declared business interests in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).
Punay said the Vice President’s name did not appear on the General Information Sheets (GIS) of GenCorp from 2022 to 2025.
Likewise, Punay said the Vice President did not receive dividends in those years since there were no dividends declared by the firm.
But upon further questioning of the senator-judges, she said that the P2.14 million was given to Duterte.
Senator-judge Francis Pangilinan said that Punay was wrong in saying that Duterte had no participation in GenCorp; being a recipient of a payout makes her a beneficiary.

During cross-examination of private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan, the defense witness also said that GenCorp has not issued an official or any public statement disputing Duterte's declaration that she is one of GenCorp’s stockholders.
Punay said it was not her responsibility to inform GenCorp about Duterte's SALN declarations identifying the company as one of her business interests, even after she assumed the vice presidency.

"I believe that my function as counsel of GenCorp [does not include] looking at other people's SALNs and adjusting our records just because somebody declared that he [or she] is a stockholder of our corporation," she said.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said an apparent conflict of interest situation has emerged from Punay’s testimony because GenCorp paid P2.14 million to Duterte and at the same time bagged P33 million worth of government contracts from the Davao City government led by the Vice President’s brother, Mayor Sebastian Duterte.
“So mukhang conflict of interest… Dahil sa kabilang banda, ‘yung investment binabayaran, ‘yung kita sa investment. Sa kabilang banda naman, nagbebenta ng pagkain sa Davao LGU,” he said.
(So it appears to be a conflict of interest because, on one hand, the returns on the investment are being paid, while on the other, the company is selling food to the Davao City government.)

Meanwhile, Punay also said that Duterte has no participation in Metro City Chow’s company affairs even if the company’s GIS from 2022 to 2025 lists her as a member of the Board of Directors and a member of the compensation committee.
“She did not participate…I have not seen her in the meetings, either board meetings or even company parties, even in the store, in the branch,” she said.
The witness also claimed that Duterte does not participate in the decision-making process, the operational management, or in the administration of the properties of the company. —LDF, GMA News

ANTALYA, Turkey – Leaders at the COP31 summit in Turkey are trying out a new sales pitch for climate action that is tailored to the times: do it to bolster the economy and bring down the cost of living.

The message, being repeated in the hallways and on the plenary stage of the annual UN conference, reflects efforts by organizers to capture the attention of governments wrestling with crises that have pushed global warming down the list of priorities.

Among those is rampant inflation driven in part by disruptions to Middle East crude oil shipments since the onset of the Iran war. Consumer price pressures from fuel to food were a major driver in the US midterm elections that handed control of Congress to Democrats, and are an important vulnerability for leaders across Europe, Asia and elsewhere.

“Three-quarters of humanity live in countries that import fossil fuels, hostage to price shocks they did not create and cannot control,” UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres told world leaders attending the summit on Wednesday, November 11.
“Recent conflicts make clear that this is a recipe for chronic insecurity and a cost-of-living meltdown,” he added, saying the clear solution is a shift to renewable energy.

Simon Stiell, head of the UN’s climate office, made the same point. “Today, chaos in global energy markets and climate disasters are supercharging inflation, slamming government budgets, pushing household bills up and living standards down,” he told the conference.
“The political costs of fossil fuel dependency are unforgiving. Climate action can help relieve the pressures.”
John Kerry, a former US secretary of state who has been advocating for climate action for decades, said he liked the reframing of the issue.

Climate change has become a massively divisive political issue in recent years, including in the US, where President Donald Trump last year withdrew the world’s top historical greenhouse gas emitter from international climate cooperation after calling warming a hoax.
“I think everybody who is working on climate needs to change the way they talk about it,” Kerry told reporters on the sidelines of the summit.
“I think that grouping of security, health, jobs, stability of communities and food supply are all very real and very much on people’s minds when I talk to them.”
European energy commissioner Dan Jorgensen said the approach could help build a consensus for action that could even include climate skeptics.

“Because even if you don’t believe in climate change, which I obviously do, we should be able to agree that moving away from a dependency on fossils is extremely smart for security reasons,” he said. – Rappler.com

Some areas of British Columbia have been without power since late last week after a series of storms rolled through, with more than 400,000 customers in total left without power between Friday and Monday, according to B.C. Hydro.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) has maintained a number of rainfall and wind warnings throughout B.C. on Wednesday, saying more than 250 millimetres of rain is possible for parts of western and inland Vancouver Island.
Flood watches are also in place throughout southwest B.C., as officials warn drivers to be prepared for pooling water and debris on the South Coast after the storm made landfall on Tuesday.

articles.title: DSWD: More than 1,300 vendors affected by ASEAN Summit
articles.summary: The vendors whose livelihoods have been disrupted are receiving cash aid and family food packs from the Department of Social Welfare and Development

blocks.text: AYUDA. Vendors in Pasay City affected by the ASEAN Summit receive P10,000 from the Department of Social Welfare and Development on November 11, 2026.
Jelo Ritzhie Mantaring/Rappler
The vendors whose livelihoods have been disrupted are receiving cash aid and family food packs from the Department of Social Welfare and Development

MANILA, Philippines – There are more than 1,300 vendors whose livelihoods have been affected by the Philippines’ hosting of the 49th Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Summit and Related Summits, according to the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD).

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian said on Wednesday, November 11, that the Parañaque City government forwarded to the DSWD a list of vendors affected in Baclaran, a bustling market area, amid security measures implemented for the event.

The city government said street vendors are “temporarily prohibited” from operating along Roxas Boulevard and its service roads, from Redemptorist Road to Quirino Avenue, as well as the road beneath the Light Rail Transit (LRT) until November 20.

blocks.caption: Parañaque clears Baclaran roads of street vendors for ASEAN Summit

blocks.text: Since Baclaran is near Pasay City as well, the DSWD is also coordinating with the local government to identify more affected vendors in the area.

“Bagamat humihingi kami ng paumanhin sa mga naantala ang hanapbuhay dahil sa napipintong ASEAN Summit, ang direktiba ng ating Pangulo ay masigurado na mabigyan sila ng tulong pinansyal kasi alam natin na wala silang kikitain sa mga araw na ‘yon,” Gatchalian said on the sidelines of cash aid distribution in Pasay City.

(We apologize to those whose livelihoods were put on hold because of the upcoming ASEAN Summit, but the directive of the President is to ensure that they will be given financial support because we know they will not have earnings during those days.)

blocks.caption: DSWD: More than 1,300 vendors affected by ASEAN Summit

blocks.text: In Pasay City, around 50 ambulant vendors and eatery workers received P10,000 from the DSWD’s Assistance to Individuals in Crisis Situations program on Wednesday. They were also given family food packs.
It was the second batch following the aid distribution to some 30 individuals on Sunday, November 8.
Most of the beneficiaries were located along Diokno Boulevard.

“Malaking tulong na rin naman po kahit papaano…. Pagkakasyahin hangga’t walang trabaho (This is still a great help somehow. We’ll make do with it while we have no work),” said Anabel de Luna, 34. The eatery where she works temporarily closed on Monday, November 9, and may resume operations on November 20 or 21.
But others like Rizal Villaula, a 40-year-old pares cart owner, had to stop selling on October 22 amid road clearing operations. He has since entered into multiple gigs, like towing services.
Maria Joanna Cristina Samarro, a 46-year-old ambulant vendor, has been selling cigarettes for the past weeks to earn just enough for some meals.

But she took the chance to set up her table in front of the Senate building, also along Diokno Boulevard, to sell various items such as bread, coffee, and soft drinks, as protesters gathered there on Wednesday morning.
When there are no road restrictions, she can earn up to P500 a day.
Gatchalian said affected vendors in Parañaque City will receive their cash aid and food packs by Thursday, November 12.
Malacañang earlier declared November 16 to 18 as special non-working days in Metro Manila to make way for the ASEAN Summit. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Spain sees widespread disruption in first general strike for 14 years
articles.summary: Protests are also expected in the biggest cities less than three weeks before Spaniards vote in parliamentary elections.
articles.byline: Nick Beake, Guy Hedgecoe, Alba Morgade

blocks.text: Transport and other public services across Spain have faced serious disruption in the first general strike for 14 years called by the main unions over housing and the high cost of living.
Demonstrations were also planned later on Wednesday, with the biggest protests expected in Madrid and Barcelona. Spaniards are due to vote in parliamentary elections on 29 November.
The head of the big UGT labour union, Pepe Álvarez, said the strike was a success with "massive" participation, while Unai Sordo of the CC OO union said turnout was "very significant."
However, the Spanish Confederation of Business Organisations said participation was "low and uneven", depending on the areas and sectors involved.
Some of the biggest disruption on Wednesday was seen in the main industrial hubs of Madrid and the north-eastern region of Catalonia where traffic was halted on several main roads.
The interior ministry said dozens of people were arrested for a variety of incidents and Spanish reports said estate agencies had seen attacks on their offices.

The strike was triggered by widespread protests over affordable housing and rising living costs, after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from a flat in Madrid where she had lived for seven decades. She died in hospital weeks later.

Rental prices in the capital have soared in recent years. The monthly cost of a 50m sq apartment in Madrid was an average of €1,170 in October, according to property portal Idealista, while Spain's average gross monthly salary is about €2,460 (£2,056).
That amounts to nearly half the average gross salary, well above the 30% level of affordability often recommended by housing experts and public institutions.
Among those taking part in the general strike was Gonzalo Álvarez, 27, who was visiting different picket lines in central Madrid.
Although he works in sales, he has been volunteering for a housing union that tries to protect tenants and makes them aware of their rights.
The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal at the end of September "was the little fire" that sparked this protest, he told the BBC.
Álvarez knew the 87-year-old, who had faced a tripling of her rent under new landlords, and says he was deeply upset by her treatment.

He rents a small, one-bedroom flat with his girlfriend, a dental hygienist, in the city's southern Arganzuela disrict. The couple pay €1,000 between them, which means each spends about half of their salary on housing, even before other bills.
"It's absolutely crazy… with the food, with the electricity, with the water, with gas."
He sees no way of getting on the property ladder: "You have to collect an insane amount of money to be able to buy a house. So with these salaries, it's impossible."
With current rent and purchase prices, he believes buying somewhere is "completely impossible".
However, the vice-president of the CEOE, Spanish biggest business association, Miguel Garrido, criticised the strike, complaining that businesses had little to do with the price of housing.
"This is not a strike for labour-related reasons, but rather for political ones, and it is closely linked to the early calling of elections," he said.
Demonstrations were planned for some of Spain's biggest cities later in the day and the scale of support will be widely viewed as an indicator of public discontent ahead of the election.
Another reliable indicator of support for strikes is the level of demand for electricity with Spain's industrial sector.

Power usage in Spain fell by 7.5% during the early hours of Wednesday, according to data from operator Red Eléctrica. During the last general strike 14 years ago, equivalent consumption was down by more than 15%.

articles.title: Killing of journalist underscores deteriorating conditions in Ecuador
articles.summary:
Tomás Beltrán was shot dead amid gang warfare that has turned Latin American country into one of its most violent

Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when…

blocks.text: Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.

Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.

Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.

Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.
Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.

“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.

“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.

The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub, particularly through the Pacific.
Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.

“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.
“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.

Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.

While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated, a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.

There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.
Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.
“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”

articles.title: First Covid lockdowns, then alcohol to your door: rise in young Victorians with liver diseases prompts fears
articles.summary:
While young people are drinking less across the board, one expert says a small minority are actually drinking huge and damaging amounts of alcohol

  • Get our

blocks.text: Rising numbers of young people are being hospitalised with severe, irreversible liver disease, as alcohol-related hospital admissions remain above pre-pandemic levels after peaking during Covid lockdowns.

A new Burnet Institute report, commissioned by the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education (Fare), analysed nearly two decades of Victorian health data to examine the prevalence of alcohol-associated harm.
The study analysed 4,111 hospital admissions between 1 January 2017 to 30 June 2024, along with clinical data from 1 January 2010 to 30 June 2024.
When Covid lockdowns began in March 2020, treatment of alcohol-related hepatitis – a subset of liver disease – rose sharply, the data shows. They slowed after restrictions eased in late 2021.
But they have continued to be far above pre-pandemic levels.

The lead researcher, Prof Jessica Howell, said the rise correllated with a number of factors linked to the “overall stress” and “uncertainty” of lockdowns, although the report “can’t specifically tease out the causes”.
“Access to alcohol increased because you could get it delivered to your home,” she said. “So that really did lead to an escalation.”
While men made up the majority of cases, accounting for 62.5% of alcohol-linked hepatitis admissions, there was a “a sharp increase” among women.
Howell attributed the rise in excessive drinking to stress for women during Covid, “particularly on women who were primary caregivers, managing schooling, work and home.”
“A small proportion of women also were at home and at risk of being stuck in violent situations if they were enduring domestic violence. Lockdowns meant they couldn’t escape that.”
Rising numbers of young people affected

The data also revealed 14% of people admitted with alcohol-associated hepatitis statewide were aged under 35, and the report warned that a significant proportion of people with severe alcohol-related liver disease were under 40.

James O’Beirne, a professor of hepatology at Sunshine Coast university hospital and Griffith University, said he believed the trends could “undoubtedly” be identified in other states and territories with further research.
He has also noticed anecdotal evidence of such a trend in his work.

“Every week on the wards, we’ve got people under the age of 50 with very advanced liver disease and complications of cirrhosis.” O’Beirne said. “We’re seeing people being admitted in their 30s with severe liver disease.
“Women seem to be more susceptible to liver disease from alcohol than men because of their smaller body habitus.”
While the Burnet Institute’s findings appear to contradict other reports that show young people are drinking less overall, he said the previous research misses a key detail.
after newsletter promotion

“While it’s true that younger people are drinking less alcohol across the board, there’s a subset of people who, unfortunately, are drinking a lot more. A small minority of young people are actually drinking huge amounts of alcohol.”
He said he also fears the changing drinking habits of young women “is leading to very advanced liver disease at an earlier age”.

“It’s well accepted that women are now drinking much more than they used to … there’s this concept of ‘wine o’clock’ that you see on social media, which I think is driving this normalisation of regular drinking,” he said.
Howell said the numbers “haven’t returned back to normal”, and fears they may not because “a new baseline of admissions for alcohol-associated hepatitis” has been set.
Fare’s chief executive, Ayla Chorley, said the report “brings to light that alcohol-related harm is very real”.
“Alcohol harm is on the streets, in front of nightclubs and pubs, and we’re now seeing it’s happening in the home,” she said.
Chorley said the findings highlighted the need for greater harm-reduction measures, including restrictions on alcohol availability, regulation and marketing.

“The alcohol industry has been very successful at individualising this condition, saying it’s an individual choice to drink responsibly … that discounts society’s expectations and cultural norms around alcohol consumption,” she said.
“People feel like: ‘Did I do something wrong? What is wrong with me? Why can’t I stop?’ And it is absolutely not on them. It is a harmful product. It is addictive by design and by its very nature.”

articles.title: ‘We were quite surprised’: Finland’s embassy goes viral with staff training day post on Instagram
articles.summary:
After a promotion for a ‘Finnish Dinner Date’ went ‘a bit viral’, the Canberra envoy’s next post became an unlikely social media hit

  • Get our

blocks.text: The embassy of Finland in Canberra was temporarily closed on Tuesday, 10 November.
Millions of people across the world were, it turns out, quite upset by this.

A day later, with the flourish of a ribbon-cutting ceremony, the embassy reopened its doors – having garnered many millions of views on its videos, spurred memes seen by millions more and social media attention across the globe, all unexpectedly from an innocuous Instagram post about a staff training day.
“We were all having a nice planning day, then someone said ‘oh my goodness it’s gone completely viral’,” Arto Haapea, Finland’s ambassador to Australia, told Guardian Australia.

The Finnish embassy, nestled in leafy Yarralumla in Canberra’s diplomatic zone just a stone’s throw from Parliament House, isn’t exactly a tourist hotspot in the nation’s capital. Flanked by the embassies of Estonia, Singapore, Mexico and Samoa, the sleek building – all grey panelling and glass – looks more like a bank or an office block than the genesis of a bizarre social media sensation stretching from Europe and the United States to the centre of Australian politics.

blocks.caption: Photograph: Instagram/Finland in Australia

blocks.text: “The embassy of Finland in Canberra will be temporarily closed on Tuesday, 10 November 2026. Regular hours will resume on Wednesday, 11 November,” @FinlandInAustralia posted on Monday, with text over video of the northern lights glowing an eerie green.

Last week, the embassy’s other Instagram videos were getting like counts in the dozens or low hundreds. The post about the building’s opening hours has, as of time of writing, been liked 622,000 times, shared 405,000 times, and been seen by up to 10 million people worldwide.

blocks.caption: Photograph: Instagram/Finland in Australia

blocks.text: How it got picked up by Instagram’s social media algorithm, and supercharged to be seen across the world, is likely something to do with the embassy’s previous video; Haapea promoting a competition to fly single people from around the world to Helsinki for a “Finnish Dinner Date”. The dinner date video also “went a bit viral”, Haapea said, getting 8m views and 163,000 likes.
“We were quite surprised by that,” the ambassador said.

Haapea said his team hadn’t had time to do any deep analysis of why these two clips went unexpectedly viral, but he theorised that the post with the opening hours “happened to ride on the same algorithm” as the dinner date, getting even more views, and attracting influencers, companies and brands around the world to make their own videos.

blocks.caption: Photograph: Instagram/Finland in Australia

blocks.text: “POV you’re trying to enter the Embassy of Finland in Canberra but it’s 10th of November,” posted @j.ackdale, knocking on a locked door. That has 604,000 likes on Instagram at the time of writing.
“Me, all the way from Muscat, trying to get answers about the Finnish embassy in Canberra,” posted @sand_and_heels from Oman.
“I’m flying over 300 people from Finland to Australia. Hopefully the Embassy of Finland in Canberra is open today,” posted Finnish pilot @juusojelmer, to 88,000 likes.

That included Finnish politicians and ambassadors around the world, many of whom posted their own jokes, calling their colleagues or reassuring Finns in various countries that their embassies remained open. Haapea said even Finland’s foreign minister was keen to chat.

blocks.caption: The Finland embassy in Yarralumla, Canberra. Photograph: Paul Kingsley/Alamy

blocks.text: “We were done with the planning day and did a sauna with the team, and the foreign minister wanted to call about the planning day,” he said, as they filmed a video together – Haapea fresh from the sauna – promising that normal functions of the embassy would resume the next day.

On Wednesday, Canberrans from politicians to radio hosts and journalists visited the embassy, making their own social media clips live from the scene, while ordinary people tried knocking on the door or chatting to Finnish staff. A lighthearted video with a grand reopening, complete with ribbon-cutting ceremony, had to come next, Haapea said.
“We thank the international community for your fascinating interest,” the embassy posted.
As to why the interest in the first place? The ambassador said he’s still not sure.

“I think people are just looking for good news, to take their minds off all the craziness in the world. With the algorithm, and people who are good at making memes, all it took was a few big influencers to make a meme about it,” Haapea said.

articles.title: Anthony Albanese fails to mention fossil fuels in Cop summit speech
articles.summary:
Australian PM boasts of success in renewables but is criticised for not addressing the nation’s huge coal industry

  • Get our

blocks.text: Anthony Albanese said governments had a “solemn responsibility” to act on climate change in a historic speech to the UN’s climate summit, but one which failed to mention the fossil fuels driving the crisis.

The Australia prime minister landed in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya on Wednesday morning where the Cop31 talks are being presided over by his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, but hosted by Turkey.
Only moments before Albanese spoke, on the same stage the UN secretary general Antonio Guterres said unambiguously that keeping the 1.5C temperature goal alive “means no new coal”.
In a packed conference room, Turkey put on an opening ceremony of whirling traditional dancers, booming music and a film shot around the world with characters saying “We need to talk”.
“This is an historic moment for my country,” said Albanese, adding Australia was “proud to be a leader on climate action.”
“Proud to be a renewable energy leader, creating the clean industries, businesses and jobs of the future. And proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family,” he said.
Australia had pushed for a role at the climate summit, he said, “because we wanted to speak for the people of the world who need urgent action, including those from our Pacific family”.
Australia is the world’s second largest exporter of coal for burning in power stations and the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking. A fifth of the world’s exported LNG comes from Australia.

Albanese pointed to “significant successes” for the country on climate change, including doubling renewable energy generation in six years that accounted for half of the country’s electricity, and building one of the world’s biggest rooftop solar and battery markets.
Guterres and several countries are pushing for the talks to progress a proposal from last year’s Cop hosts, Brazil, for countries to develop detailed plans to move away from fossil fuels.
Guterres told the conference: “Leaders – and in particular those from developed countries – cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5 degrees.”
He said to keep the globally-agreed goal of limiting global heating to 1.5C within reach, coal power had to fall by at least 75% by 2035.
Unabated coal power – that is, coal generated without safely capturing the carbon dioxide emissions – “must be all but phased out” by 2040, and oil and gas use cut by a third, he said.

“Every government must align its policies, investments and infrastructure plans accordingly. That starts with credible national roadmaps to transition away from fossil fuels — protecting workers and communities.
“That means no new coal. No new oil and gas infrastructure that puts 1.5 degrees further out of reach.”
Guterres and he has consistently called out fossil fuel production and lobbying and the lack of action on climate change as temperatures and weather extremes have worsened.
Adam Bandt, the former Greens leader and now chief executive of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said Albanese had “bluntly ignored” the secretary general’s message.

“The prime minister’s speech wasn’t just a missed opportunity, but by refusing to rein in coal and gas expansion or even mention it once, it was a snub to the secretary general’s call to tell the truth,” he said.
“At this summit, Australia is getting repeatedly called out for opening new coal and gas mines and the government can’t dodge it forever.”
Bill Hare, the Australian chief executive of Climate Analytics and a veteran of Cop meetings, said it was “disturbing” that Albanese had failed to mention fossil fuels.
As a major fossil fuel exporter, he said a “responsible leader” would have talked about developing a pathway out of fossil fuels.
“It still seems to be a dirty word. It’s the elephant in the room,” he said, pointing to 38 fossil projects approved by the Albanese government since it was elected in 2022.
Australia and Turkey are seeking support for a global goal to see 35% of final-use energy coming from electricity by 2035 – up from about a fifth today.

Speaking during a roll-call of heads of state and world leaders, Bowen said the world was asking if multilateralism could rise to a “polycrisis” of climate change, energy security, conflict and the power demands of artificial intelligence.
“Is international cooperation still a way forward? This fortnight we can answer those legitimate concerns and questions with a simple answer: Yes,” said Bowen.

articles.title: Millions join Spain’s first general strike in 14 years in protest at rising housing costs
articles.summary:
The 24-hour stoppage has drawn high participation across sectors and comes weeks before election in which far right could gain power

Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s…
articles.byline: Ashifa Kassam in Madrid and Stephen Burgen in Barcelona

blocks.text: Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
At the centre of Wednesday’s nationwide 24-hour stoppage, singularly backed by the country’s largest unions as well as tenants’ associations, is a pushback against Spain’s deepening housing crisis.

Sandra Mora, of the Madrid Tenants’ Union, told the broadcaster RNE: “It’s extremely important to remind people that we, the workers – who are also renters or who also pay mortgages – are the ones with the power to halt production and bring the economy to a standstill.”

While workers’ unions reported high participation in the strike across several sectors, including 90% in the automotive and port sectors and 82% in waste collection, they said participation was uneven across the country. The strongest support was reported in coastal regions, such as Catalonia and Andalusia, where the soaring cost of housing has been particularly acute.

Many schools and universities were reportedly closed or working at minimal capacity. In Madrid, the labour action added to an ongoing strike by teachers that began nearly a month ago to demand better working conditions.

In Barcelona, workers set up roadblocks – some with burning tyres – as public transport came to a near-standstill. In Madrid, scuffles broke out between picketers and police near the country’s main wholesale market, while demonstrators dragged ⁠large recycling bins on to the streets to block traffic. By midday on Wednesday, government officials said 27 people had been arrested over minor incidents across the country.

blocks.caption: Protesters set fire to tyres at a roadblock on Wednesday in Barcelona. Photograph: Andreu Dalmau/EPA

blocks.text: Stormy weather loomed over the plans for afternoon marches across the country after Spain’s state meteorological agency issued 14 alerts for two storms that were expected to bring strong winds, rough seas and heavy rains.

The long-simmering frustration at soaring housing prices across Spain burst into public view in September after the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the home in which she had lived for more than seven decades.

As protests and encampments sprang up across Spain, it cast a spotlight on a market where properties were increasingly being used as tourist lets, speculative assets and short-term rentals, sending rents rising by 80% within a decade while the cost of homes climbed by 63%.

Before Wednesday’s strike, the tenants’ union of Granada sought to highlight this link, descending on the city’s most touristed areas to vandalise about 300 lockboxes belonging to short-term rentals. “No to capitalists, no to rent-seekers, no to their accomplices,” the organisation wrote on social media, as they posted pictures of lockboxes that had been rendered unusable.

blocks.caption: An estate agents’ office in Móstoles, Madrid, covered with stickers calling on people to join the general strike. Photograph: Angel Perez/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Housing campaigners and unions have called on the government to do more to intervene in the market, with tenants’ unions demanding measures such as limits on the evictions of vulnerable people, rent freezes and a crackdown on short-term rentals.
Unai Sordo, the head of one of the country’s biggest labour unions, the Workers’ Commissions, told Cadena Ser radio: “There is one issue that is dividing the country: the struggle to access housing.”

Spain is holding a general election on 29 November. The snap vote was called by the Socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, after rightwing parties torpedoed emergency legislation aimed at tackling the housing crisis.
after newsletter promotion
Polls suggest the most likely outcome will be a rightwing coalition between the People’s party and the far-right, anti-immigration Vox party.

While Sánchez has sought to focus the campaign on social issues, the discussion has shifted to questions over infrastructure after at least 69 people were killed in Spain’s second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year.

This week Sánchez seized on the strike, whose official slogan is “Salaries. Housing. Prices”, as a way to recast the spotlight, posting a video in which he lauded developments such as the eight-hour workday and national health insurance and credited them to the labour movement and the right to strike. “It wasn’t easy, but they changed Spain,” Sánchez said.

blocks.caption: Teachers protest at a metro station in Madrid on Wednesday. Photograph: JJ Guillen/EPA

blocks.text: His position sharply contrasted with the discourse of parties on the right who, in the lead-up to the strike, said unions were trying to help Sánchez remain in office.

This week the rightwing leader of the Madrid region, Isabel Díaz Ayuso, accused striking workers of “holding citizens hostage”. Ayuso, who this year faced questions over her administration’s decision to allegedly spend €6.3m (£5.4m) of public funds on a residential penthouse to use as a temporary office, added: “Everything is chaotic, everything is gridlocked.”

While she acknowledged that union activity is a constitutional right, she also said she had vented her frustrations to the leader of the People’s party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who polls suggest will be the next prime minister. “I’ll confess something,” she told Spanish television. “I spoke to Feijóo and I told him: ‘Promise me this garbage will end.’”

articles.title: Italy: Hundreds of schools evacuated after bomb threats
articles.summary: Although the government believes the threat to be a hoax, it has nevertheless prompted concerns about "hybrid warfare" in Europe. Similar messages were sent in Northern Ireland, Ireland, and Bulgaria.

image.caption: Police arrived at schools in Milan and other cities in ItalyImage: Luca Bruno/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: At 10 a.m. local time on Wednesday, 312 Italian schools received the same e-mail: "A powerful explosive device with a remote detonator has been left in your building."
Most of the affected schools were in Rome, but several other major cities also got the same message.
Antonello Giannelli, head of the National Association of School Principals, said that it was "clearly the work of a hoaxer" trying to sow chaos.
Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said it was also designed to "sow terror" for thousands of families.

blocks.caption: Schools in Naples were also among those affectedImage: Sergio Siano/IPA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's cabinet will convene an emergency meeting this afternoon, the Palazzo Chigi has confirmed.
"The government is closely monitoring the numerous reports of bomb threats at schools," Meloni said in a statement posted to social media.
"Law enforcement agencies and government institutions at every level are working to monitor the situation and reassure citizens, families, and school staff.
"At this time, based on the investigations conducted, there is no evidence to suggest that a concrete danger exists. Rather, the reports appear to be part of a strategy aimed at causing alarm."
Concerns over hybrid warfare
The threatening e-mail sent to Italian schools was signed with the same fake name as similar messages that went out to newsrooms in Bulgaria and Ireland on Friday.
Some 300 schools in Northern Ireland were also affected, though it was immediately clear if the threats had come from the same sender.

Recent hybrid attacks on supermarkets, air traffic controllers, blood banks and broadcasters across Europe have raised worries amongst leaders that this may be part of a coordinated attempt at hybrid warfare.
France summoned the Iranian ambassador on Tuesday over cyberattacks that caused supermarket freezers to defrost, but Tehran has denied any involvement.

Crosetto also cautioned against jumping to conclusions, saying: "It is not always ​the work of foreign countries or hostile entities. There are also attention-seekers and lunatics who" simply want to unleash mayhem.

articles.title: Tundu Lissu: After escaping the death penalty, what does his guilty verdict mean for Tanzania's democracy?
articles.summary: A treason trial could have meant death by hanging for Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu. Instead, he now faces four years in prison for incitement to unrest. Ban dissident voices truly be heard…
articles.byline: Eddy Micah Jr., Imani Henrick Luvanga, Isaac Mugabi, Benita van Eyssen

image.caption: Opposition figure Tundu Lissu originally faced the death penalty for treasonImage: ChademaTZ2/X

blocks.text: On November 6, Tundu Lissu, leader of Tanzania's main opposition Chadema party, was sentenced to four years in prison for incitement following heavy unrest during the October 2025 elections.
The same day, he was cleared of treason charges — which could have meant a death sentence if he had been found guilty.

Lissu commented that the judiciary had acted under pressure; he rejected the verdict due to the fact that incitement was not among the charges which had brought against him at the start of his trial in 2025.
Chadema officials have now signaled an intention to appeal the court decision. The government has not issued a statement on his conviction yet.

blocks.caption: Police officers also detained several of Lissu's supporters during clashes in April 2025Image: Emmanuel Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Tanzania's most dramatic trial in decades

Few opposition figures have shaped modern Tanzanian politics as dramatically as Lissu. A lawyer by training and one of the country's most outspoken critics of the ruling party Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), Lissu has spent years challenging the political establishment.

Over the years, he has been subjected to repeated arrest and detention; in 2017, he survived an attempt on his life by unknown gunmen outside his residence in the capital Dodoma, sustaining multiple bullet wounds.

More recently, his trial in the run-up to the October 2025 general election continued to keep him and the opposition in the public eye following his arrest in April 2025 in the southwestern town of Mbinga.
Why was Tundu Lissu arrested?
Prosecuters accused Lissu of encouraging the public to prevent the 2025 election from taking place and charged him with one count of treason.
As legal evidence, they cited social media posts he had made, in which he was seen to be calling on Tanzanians to boycott the vote over concerns about possible electoral malpractice.
In the end, the election went ahead without Chadema on October 29, which was marred by violence on an unprecedented in scale in Tanzania; security forces even used live ammunition on protesters.

Francis Ibrahim, an independent political analyst based in Dar es Salaam, told DW that "heads have to roll from the law enforcement side, who overstretched their mandate, all the way to the people, who financed, planned and organized [this crackdown]."
But after a nationwide internet shutdown and curfew following the election violence, incumbent President Samia Suluhu Hassan was named winner with 98% of the vote.
Tanzania's post-election violence: No justice after a year
What does the verdict mean for democracy?
Ibrahim believes that the removal of the capital treason charge could be interpreted as a move towards rapprochment with voters.
"What I can tell you is that they are looking for a political deescalation that could solve the crisis," he explained, adding that Lissu might yet get to have a small say in politics after all:

"There has to be a process of [creating] a new constitution, and it needs everybody on the table," he said, adding that Lissu might therefore perhaps be released early in order to partake in discussions and negotiations.

However when in late July, President Suluhu Hassan met with representatives of more than a dozen political parties to discuss national reconciliation and constitutional reform, Chadema officials were explicitly not party to the consultations.
German lawmakers press Tanzania over rights concerns
Politics at play behind the verdict?
Public opinion meanwhile varies on Lissu's verdict, with many Tanzanians however saying that the trial was politically motivated in their view.
Ruqaya Mohammed, the National Deputy Secretary of the oppsition ACT-Wazalendo party's youth wing, told DW, "ee are getting into a darker space in our political arena."
"I think it's the right time now, as a nation, to have open dialogue on some reforms, on the legal perspective and electoral reforms. Maybe if we manage ... that, we can see a light," she explained.

blocks.caption: Security forces were deployed during the Tundu Lissu trial in Dar es Salaam, with the mandate to ensure public orderImage: Emmanuel Herman/REUTERS

blocks.text: Most others, however, remain reluctant to go on record for fear of reprisal; a musician and human rights advocate was among few who agreed to speak to DW — on the strict condition of anonymity.

In his view, Tanzanians simply are not free to express themselves publicly at all: "You saw the terror atmosphere and climate of fear outside the court premises when Tundu's judgement was ... read. Such is the broader display of what Tanzania looks like," he told DW.

"Opposition politics has been suppressed for years, and his conviction is just a continuation of what has been happening. It's a miracle that he is still alive. To put him in jail from four years is far from the worst-case scenario."
Youth turn to digital activism as Tanzania clamps down
This article has been adapted from an episode of DW's AfricaLink podcast.
